Various tests were discussed earlier (Chapter 6.2.2) under the heading “Training Intensity, Heart Rate and Other 
Tests” to introduce tests which can be helpful in assessing physical work capacity in strength athletes and this 
information should be regarded as an extension of that earlier material.
One of the other methods used by Russian coaches is the cardiac function Shtanga Functional Pressure test 
to ascertain if the athlete is overtraining (described by Vyurberg, 1953). Because it involves breath holding and 
rapid expulsion of air, this test is regarded as being particularly suitable for athletes like Olympic weightlifters 
and wrestlers, whose sports require them to strain against heavy resistance. This test requires the athlete to 
breath in relaxed fashion for a few minutes, then inhaling maximally and holding the breath for 15-20 seconds 
before stopping the nose and exhaling as forcibly as possible for 2 seconds. This action is accompanied by a 
sharp rise in intrathoracic pressure and diminished flow of blood to the heart.
Blood pressure is measured before the test (BPl), immediately afterwards (BP2), and after 2 minutes of 
relaxed breathing (BP3), since the purpose of this test is to analyse changes in blood pressure (BP). Systolic 
blood pressure increases significantly during the recuperation stage after the disturbance in cardiac activity by the 
test. If the contractile processes of the myocardium are normal, as in the well-prepared athlete who is not 
exhibiting chronic fatigue, the blood pressure decreases briefly by 5- 10mm Hg.
Research conducted by Ulchcnko (1982) among elite weightlifters during their specific preparation stage for 
competition applied this test in the following manner:
Test I: BPl, BP2 and BP3 measured before training
Test 2: The same three BP measures were taken during the most intense training loading 
This work produced the following interpretations of the findings
1. BP decrease after Test 1 or no change after Test 2. This is regarded as an excellent reaction.
2. BP increase of up to 5mm Hg immediately after Test 2 and recovery of normal BP after 2 minutes rest. 
This is considered to be a good reaction.
3. BP increase of up to 7mm Hg after Test 2 and 5 minutes recovery time. This is regarded as satisfactory.
4. BP increase of 10mm Hg or more after Test 2 and prolonged elevation of BP afterwards. This is regarded 
as an unsatisfactory response and is associated with an overtraining state.
The individual results for one of the weightlifters involved in this study is very instructional. This athlete 
reported feeling fit and strong and his RPE (Rating of Perceived Effort) was low during non-maximal loads (with 
exercises including clean pulls and back squats), but the Shtanga Test revealed that the actual functional state of 
the lifter was below par. The results for his analysis were:
Test I: BPl was 130/70, BP2 was 140/75 and BP3 was 135/70. The 10mm increase in BP after the pressure test 
was regarded as unsatisfactory.
Test 2: BPl was 140/66, BP2 was 160/70 and BP3 was 142/70. The 20mm increase in BP after the pressure test 
significantly exceeded the initial value and this also indicated an unsatisfactory response.
Interestingly, this lifter and several others whose pressure tests were deemed to be unacceptable did not improve 
their results in the competition which followed these tests and their coaches were advised to modify their training 
programmes until the pressure tests indicated a better functional state.

function may certainly be relevant to the Olympic weightlifter and other strength athletes. He considered that

repetitions, sets and sessions). An otherwise carefully-devised training programme is of little value if it causes 
injury to the athlete.
Injuries may be caused by accident or overtraining. The former often depends on factors which lie outside 
the direct control of the athlete and concern dangers arising unexpectedly in the environment or through the 
actions of other competitors. Nevertheless, thorough physical preparation, astute situation analysis, training of 
reactive ability, efficient ongoing interpretation of feedback from cucs provided by other players or the 
environment, and good anticipation can prove invaluable in minimising the risks posed by accident or unexpected 
events in sport.

.... There is only a dangerous way o f doing any exercise. Is this a valid general rule? While it is very often true, 
we also have to note that:

• The most recent exercise or activity can be the final trigger
• Injuries may be the result of “too much, too soon” of a safe thing (overtraining)
• Injuries may be causcd by inadequate pre-exercise preparation (“warm-up”)
• Accidents happen
• Cause and effect are not linearly related
• Individual responses to exercise are different
• Injuries arc context or situation dependent

son-traumatic cause of injuries. They, together with several medical experts, assert that there is no clinical

dimage caused by lack of suppleness, faulty technique, inappropriate footwear and so on.

aad at any given instant - “too heavy” ) and overuse (too large a quantity of work or exercise - “too much”)

The stifTcr spring A, in absorbing the energy E, is forced to its elastic limit at a, whereas the less stiff spring B 
extends further to C, but reaches nowhere near its elastic limit at b. It is possible, too, that certain individuals may 
have similar tissue stiffness but higher elastic limits. Again, the result will be a superior ability to absorb energy as 
imposed for instance .on the soft tissues of the knee by running, jumping or squatting (Siff 1982a, b). This 
analysis is particularly relevant to an understanding of tendon injuries, since much of the muscle activity in 
running is associated with tensioning of the tendons to store energy, a process which involves little length change 
in the muscic fibres themselves (Alexander et al, 1967).

limit is the same for both springs. The shaded area up to a is the same as the shaded area up to c and represents the energy absorbed. E 
(SifT 1982a, b)
Instead of referring solely to "overtraining injuries" it might be more valuable to talk of "exercise imbalance 
injuries". Such a term would embrace any form of unbalanced training, be it excessive, drug assisted or technically 
faulty.
The occurrence of "exercise imbalance injuries" may then be described scientifically on the basis of a 
qualitative topological model, called Catastrophe Theory by its inventor. Prof Rene Thom (Woodcock & Davis, 
1980). Theories which consider overtraining to be a gradual, continuous change from health to injury do not 
adequately describe the abrupt appearance of some overtraining injuries.
Catastrophe theory uses abstract multi-dimensional surfaces to describe such changes of state. It provides a 
behaviour surface, something like a buckled carpct, whose characteristics (such as its shape) are determined by 
one or more control dimensions. In the case of joint or general body stability the behaviour surface describes the 
state of health of the joint or body. The nature of this behaviour surface may be regarded as depending on the 
following four control factors:
Structural Predisposition to Injury: This depends on heredity, structural changes caused by previous exercise, 
earlier injuries, ageing and so on.
Technique Stress: This is stress caused by faulty technique, posture and equipment, including footwear.
463
#### PDF 475
SUPERTRAINING
Physical Stress: This conccms the exercisc load and frequency, current illness, adequacy of sleep, and 
environmental conditions (such as temperature and altitude).
Psychological Stress: There are several different types o f catastrophe structure, depending on the number of 
behaviour and control dimensions. In the case under discussion there is one dimension o f behaviour (state of 
health) and the four control dimensions given above, so that the appropriate system would be a "butterfly 
catastrophe". To depict this requires a 5 - dimensional drawing, which is impossible. However, if the four control 
dimensions are reduced to two by keeping two of them constant (e.g. psychological stress and technique stress), a 
useful version of the "butterfly” surface may be sketched (Fig 8.9).
Figure 8.9 Butterfly Catastrophe Model of the Injury Process (Siff 1982a, b)
Consider someone with a predisposition to injury. This athlete’s state before commencing exercise will be 
represented by point A. As the level of physical stress increases, so will the body progress towards a state of 
exhaustion at B. The natural tendency then will be to relax slightly to a more comfortable level back along path 
AB towards the initial state A, then to produce re-exertion and repeat the process back and forth within the limits 
of individual endurance.
A person with a very high predisposition to injury may begin exercising in a state G and without suffering 
undue stress may reach the threshold H. Any small increase in training load, however, may precipitate him 
without significant physical warning into the injured state at J. This is vital to remember, since damage may be 
occurring constantly and insidiously without producing pain signals. Often pain occurs when it is too late to take 
evasive action. This is especially true of the cumulative damage caused by years of executing very stressful 
exercises in terms of either intensity, volume or both.
The extent and location of the butterfly fold depends on the individual and may be influenced, for example, 
by appropriate supplementary training, medical treatment or ergogenic aids (drugs or supplements).
Consider now the individual who may begin a sporting career in a state C. Under moderate stress this athlete 
may progress to the critical point D and become trapped for prolonged periods in a region of the butterfly fold in
464
#### PDF 476
SUPERTRAINING
istate of chronic injury which rest or medical attention may rectify, but only as long as the stressful activity 
ifch caused the injury is discontinued.
The person with very low predisposition to injury is not necessarily immune to overtraining or exercise 
lance injury. For instance, he may ignore the usual symptoms of exhaustion while approaching state B and 
progress towards an injured state such as F. This type of individual, characterized by intense motivation, may 
m shift the body's initial state from A towards C or increase the extent of the fold by training in a state of 
•jjidual stress caused by inadequate rest.
Different combinations of any two control dimensions may be selected as the variables instead of 
predisposition to injury" and "physical stress". In this way the athlete and coach can appreciate the importance 
of the four control dimensions (given earlier) in planning a training routine to minimize occurrence of exercise 
unbalance or overtraining injuries. The athlete should rely on objective and subjective tests to identify personal 
aaracteristic paths of operation on the behaviour surface and avoid exercising or competing too close to the 
atastrophe fold (Siff 1982a, b).
General B io m e c h a n ic a l C a u s e s o f In ju ry
The general biomechanical causes of injury may be summarised as follows:
1. The force or stress component (force per unit area o f tissue) on some part of the body is excessive in a 
particular direction (this may be caused by very large mass or very large acceleration)
2. The torque or moment about a ccrtain pivot or joint is excessive
3. Momentum is too great to be adequately utilised or dissipated
4. The work load or energy involved over a given period is excessive
5. The power generated by the muscles is excessive at a particular instant
6. The strain (change in relative length, AL/L) in any tissues is excessive
7. The mechanical properties of any given tissues are inadequate to handle the loading
8. The Rate of Force Development (RFD) is excessive at a particular instant
9. Frictional forces are too large (mat bums or jerkiness) or too small (slipping)
These general categories may be expanded to identify some more specific causes of injury:
• Inappropriate warming up (pre-activity preparation) or stretching
• Inappropriate or inefficient patterns of movement
• Unsafe use of momentum to execute a movement
• Excessive range of movement for a particular joint
• Inappropriate phases of muscular tension or relaxation
• Use of inappropriate soft tissues for a particular action
• Magnitude of acceleration or deceleration is too great
• Imposition of an excessive load on any part of the body
• Use of inappropriate sequences of exercises
• Excessive exertion during exhaustion, distress, illness or injury
• Use of inadequate rest, recovery time or methods of recuperation
• Use of inappropriate or faulty equipment
• Excessive impact forces on body parts making contact with an object or surface
• Inappropriate or inefficient breathing patterns
• Excessive duration of any activity.
• Inability to effectively interpret and use proprioceptive and other sensory feedback
• Inability to effectively visualize, predict or use feedforward
• Inefficient use of breathing or breath-holding patterns
With particular reference to injuries produced by inefficient patterns of movement, one must appreciate that 
deviations from normal patterns may be caused by:
• Pain, soreness, stiffness or discomfort
• Muscle weakness or imbalance between muscle groups
465
#### PDF 477
SUPERTRAINING
• Any limitation in the range of joint range of movement in any direction
• Uncoordinated movement
• Musculoskeletal changes
• Fatigue
• Changes in surface, footwear, equipment or environment
• Neural changes
• Visual or balance changes
• Emotional disturbance.
It is necessary to dispel the belief that all injuries are accompanied by pain. In many cases, such as disintegration 
of cartilages and hyperflexion damage to the spine, the onset of pain may occur only once the injury has become 
extensive or serious. Microruptures of soft tissue or similar minor injuries may be unheralded by pain signals 
until they have accumulated over a sufficiently long period to incapacitate the athlete. Overtraining or regular 
impact (e.g. caused by running on hard surfaces or by blows to the head in contact sports) are associated with 
this insidious type of injury process. Individual perception of pain differs markedly among individuals or under 
different emotional or fatigue states, so that it is unreliable to use the perception of pain to assess the safety of 
any exercise.
However, it should be noted that the perception of pain by the central nervous system (CNS) can reorganise 
the motor control system to minimise the pain, which can result in reflex inhibition o f the musclcs to exert 
maximal strength and thereby lead to muscle weakness (Stokes & Young, 1984). In fact, even if the injury is not 
accompanied by pain, this can also occur. This is very common with even relatively insubstantial injuries of the 
knee such as patellar tendinitis, pcripatcllar pain syndrome or chondromalacia patellae, which significantly reduce 
the ability o f the quadriceps to produce powerful contraction. 
It is possible that the pain caused by muscle 
swelling or delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) may also provoke the CNS into responding with alternative 
motor programs which distribute force production over a larger number of muscle fibres and diminish the 
efficiency and magnitude of strength output (Stauber, 1989). The importance of dealing with even minor pain, 
soreness or injury then becomes obvious.
In the light of current paranoia about the dangers of certain exercises, it is vital to appreciate that the lack of 
safety in exercise is not simply a consequence o f so-called dangerous exercises, but also one o f unsafe execution of 
any exercise. Exercise safety must always be viewed in the context of the overall training session or programme 
for each specific individual. While ccrtain exercises may be intrinsically less safe for the relative novice to training, 
they may pose minimal risks for the same person after several months of training. 
Conversely, the least 
demanding and simplest of exercises may cause serious injury to an elite athlete who is careless, unmotivated or 
overtrained.
For beginners it is undoubtedly preferable to err on the side o f conservatism. In doing so, one should 
remember that religious avoidance of certain exercises can lead to an overall imbalance between muscle groups or 
in motor coordination and increase the likelihood of injury during the sports event. Furthermore, the avoidance 
of exercising a muscle group in a particular way never enhances safety; it simply weakens those muscles relative 
to the exercise pattern which is avoided.
Injury Prevention by Imperfection Training
The occurrence o f injury is partly related to the philosophy of injury prevention. Currently, the emphasis is 
placed almost exclusively on prevention by means of avoidance of so-called 'dangerous' exercises and excessive 
volumes or intensities o f loading. Unfortunately, this approach is limited in that it tends to neglect the vital 
aspect o f preparation to cope with less than optimal training and competitive situations. 
All-round sports 
training must include the capability o f coping with unexpected and sub-optimal conditions. In certain sports where 
accidents or unexpected situations often occur, such as the martial arts, parachuting and motor racing, 
participants are taught how to cope with events that can have serious consequences. This type of preparation 
needs to be adopted far more extensively in all sports so that the athlete is able to anticipate threatening 
situations, react much more rapidly to unexpected circumstances, take action to avoid or minimise injury, and 
cope with sub-optimal conditions by practising with imperfectly executed movements.
These strategies are rarely invoked, but they should be a standard item in the training repertoire of every 
athlete. After all, it is rarely possible to produce perfection of movement every time or to balance one's training 
loads very precisely, so it is logical to programme the nervous system and brain to respond with effective
466
#### PDF 478
SUPERTRAJNING
contingency actions whenever imperfections of movement or accidents occur. For instance, it is not unusual to 
witness Russian wcightlifters holding a snatch overhead in the low squat position and shifting in different 
directions to move the bar into unstable positions which they are then compelled to control by astute postural 
adjustments.
In general, exercise safety is largely a consequence of skill development (neuromuscular efficiency) and may 
be enhanced by imposing activities which progress carefully with respect to factors such as complexity, 
intensity, volume, speed, range of movement, duration, variety, level of fatigue and mental state.
8.9 Safety and Training Apparel
8.9.1 Lifting, B elts and Breathing
The weightlifting belt has persisted in its existing form ever since Olympic Weightlifting emerged as a sport. 
Those who use it claim that it definitely supports the back; those who do not, state catcgorically that their backs 
are strong enough not to rely on external support. Many lifters believe that a belt is necessary for the clean-and- 
jerk alone, even though in the snatch their backs arc being called upon to support more than three-quarters of the 
weight lifted in the jerk. Some authorities regard the benefits of the belt to be mainly psychological.
Who is correct? What is the truth behind use of the lifting belt? To answer these questions, it is necessary to 
analyse the physiology and biomechanics of the trunk during lifting, as well as the traditional design o f the 
present belt.

musclcs below it tells you a lot about the tension in the muscles, the pressure in your abdomen and the

directly supporting any load that you may hold overhead, other than limiting the tendency to hyperextend the

posture and the downward force is exerted through the joints (including ligaments, cartilages and discs) to the

faulty.

qualitative topological model, called Catastrophe Theory by its inventor. Prof Rene Thom (Woodcock & Davis, 
1980). Theories which consider overtraining to be a gradual, continuous change from health to injury do not 
adequately describe the abrupt appearance of some overtraining injuries.

behaviour surface, something like a buckled carpct, whose characteristics (such as its shape) are determined by 
one or more control dimensions. In the case of joint or general body stability the behaviour surface describes the 
state of health of the joint or body. The nature of this behaviour surface may be regarded as depending on the 
following four control factors:
Structural Predisposition to Injury: This depends on heredity, structural changes caused by previous exercise, 
earlier injuries, ageing and so on.
Technique Stress: This is stress caused by faulty technique, posture and equipment, including footwear.

Physical Stress: This conccms the exercisc load and frequency, current illness, adequacy of sleep, and 
environmental conditions (such as temperature and altitude).

behaviour and control dimensions. In the case under discussion there is one dimension o f behaviour (state of 
health) and the four control dimensions given above, so that the appropriate system would be a "butterfly 
catastrophe". To depict this requires a 5 - dimensional drawing, which is impossible. However, if the four control 
dimensions are reduced to two by keeping two of them constant (e.g. psychological stress and technique stress), a 
useful version of the "butterfly” surface may be sketched (Fig 8.9).
Figure 8.9 Butterfly Catastrophe Model of the Injury Process (Siff 1982a, b)
Consider someone with a predisposition to injury. This athlete’s state before commencing exercise will be 
represented by point A. As the level of physical stress increases, so will the body progress towards a state of 
exhaustion at B. The natural tendency then will be to relax slightly to a more comfortable level back along path 
AB towards the initial state A, then to produce re-exertion and repeat the process back and forth within the limits 
of individual endurance.
A person with a very high predisposition to injury may begin exercising in a state G and without suffering 
undue stress may reach the threshold H. Any small increase in training load, however, may precipitate him 
without significant physical warning into the injured state at J. This is vital to remember, since damage may be 
occurring constantly and insidiously without producing pain signals. Often pain occurs when it is too late to take 
evasive action. This is especially true of the cumulative damage caused by years of executing very stressful 
exercises in terms of either intensity, volume or both.
The extent and location of the butterfly fold depends on the individual and may be influenced, for example, 
by appropriate supplementary training, medical treatment or ergogenic aids (drugs or supplements).
Consider now the individual who may begin a sporting career in a state C. Under moderate stress this athlete 
may progress to the critical point D and become trapped for prolonged periods in a region of the butterfly fold in

lance injury. For instance, he may ignore the usual symptoms of exhaustion while approaching state B and 
progress towards an injured state such as F. This type of individual, characterized by intense motivation, may 
m shift the body's initial state from A towards C or increase the extent of the fold by training in a state of 
•jjidual stress caused by inadequate rest.

predisposition to injury" and "physical stress". In this way the athlete and coach can appreciate the importance

unbalance or overtraining injuries. The athlete should rely on objective and subjective tests to identify personal 
aaracteristic paths of operation on the behaviour surface and avoid exercising or competing too close to the 
atastrophe fold (Siff 1982a, b).

The general biomechanical causes of injury may be summarised as follows:
1. The force or stress component (force per unit area o f tissue) on some part of the body is excessive in a 
particular direction (this may be caused by very large mass or very large acceleration)
2. The torque or moment about a ccrtain pivot or joint is excessive
3. Momentum is too great to be adequately utilised or dissipated
4. The work load or energy involved over a given period is excessive
5. The power generated by the muscles is excessive at a particular instant
6. The strain (change in relative length, AL/L) in any tissues is excessive
7. The mechanical properties of any given tissues are inadequate to handle the loading
8. The Rate of Force Development (RFD) is excessive at a particular instant
9. Frictional forces are too large (mat bums or jerkiness) or too small (slipping)
These general categories may be expanded to identify some more specific causes of injury:
• Inappropriate warming up (pre-activity preparation) or stretching
• Inappropriate or inefficient patterns of movement
• Unsafe use of momentum to execute a movement
• Excessive range of movement for a particular joint
• Inappropriate phases of muscular tension or relaxation
• Use of inappropriate soft tissues for a particular action
• Magnitude of acceleration or deceleration is too great
• Imposition of an excessive load on any part of the body
• Use of inappropriate sequences of exercises
• Excessive exertion during exhaustion, distress, illness or injury
• Use of inadequate rest, recovery time or methods of recuperation
• Use of inappropriate or faulty equipment
• Excessive impact forces on body parts making contact with an object or surface
• Inappropriate or inefficient breathing patterns
• Excessive duration of any activity.
• Inability to effectively interpret and use proprioceptive and other sensory feedback
• Inability to effectively visualize, predict or use feedforward
• Inefficient use of breathing or breath-holding patterns
With particular reference to injuries produced by inefficient patterns of movement, one must appreciate that 
deviations from normal patterns may be caused by:

• Muscle weakness or imbalance between muscle groups
465
#### PDF 477
SUPERTRAINING
• Any limitation in the range of joint range of movement in any direction
• Uncoordinated movement
• Musculoskeletal changes
• Fatigue
• Changes in surface, footwear, equipment or environment

of cartilages and hyperflexion damage to the spine, the onset of pain may occur only once the injury has become 
extensive or serious. Microruptures of soft tissue or similar minor injuries may be unheralded by pain signals

accompanied by pain, this can also occur. This is very common with even relatively insubstantial injuries of the 
knee such as patellar tendinitis, pcripatcllar pain syndrome or chondromalacia patellae, which significantly reduce

topic: training to avoid injury
category: [injury-prevention, reactive-ability, skill, contact-sports]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-10-13

# Prepare Athletes for the Risky Movements Their Sport Contains Instead of Banning Them: Train Reaction, Anticipation and Falling

**What it is** — Under "Training to Avoid Injury" the authors write: "Avoidance of certain exercises which are regarded as potentially harmful may sometimes be unwise, because those very movements may occur periodically in the sport or during practice. This well-meaning approach can predispose athletes to injury since they will not have acquired the necessary involuntary motor skills to cope with higher risk actions. Therefore, it can be valuable to progressively introduce skills intended to prepare the athlete to minimise the chance of accidents and injury" (PDF 439 / p.428, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is skill: an athlete never exposed to a high-risk action lacks the "involuntary motor skills to cope" when the sport forces it. "Training of reactive ability can be extremely helpful in this regard, although too many athletes strengthen the body instead to achieve this end. It would be far better for them to improve speed of reaction, speed of movement, ability to anticipate impending dangers and to learn to manage dangerous events while they are happening" (PDF 439 / p.428).

**When to apply** — When a movement is dropped from a programme as "dangerous" but the sport still produces it (contact, falls, awkward landings). Introduce it "progressively." The authors' contact-sport case: "It is surprising how few rugby and American football players never learn how to fall from their colleagues in judo and wrestling, yet falling and violent bodily contact are integral parts of their games" (PDF 439 / p.428; the double negative "how few ... never" is printed so, and the sense is that few learn to fall). Eric's review: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the book's "progressively introduce" matches that rule; exposure is graded, not sudden.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors say avoidance "may sometimes be unwise," not always; a movement the sport does not contain is not covered. No injury data are given. "Too many athletes strengthen the body instead" sets reactive skill against strength, but the book does not say strength work is useless for injury risk. Inference: in a rehab or novice setting, holding back a high-risk movement until basic control is present is still graded exposure, not the avoidance the authors criticise.

**Example** — The authors' own: teaching rugby and American football players the falling skills used in judo and wrestling, since falling and contact are part of their games (PDF 439 / p.428).

**Related** — [[principle--return-to-play-incomplete-until-the-athlete-perceives-full-healing]], [[heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-only-unsafe-execution-for-individual]], [[claim--reaction-time-mostly-fixed-movement-time-trainable]], [[heuristic--progressive-and-random-segmental-training]]

# There Is No Single "Optimal" Quadriceps:Hamstring Ratio: It Changes With Sport, Joint Angle and Test Velocity

**What it is** — It is often claimed the optimal quadriceps-to-hamstring strength ratio is
60:40, but Russian scientists found this ratio depends on the specific sport (Vorobyev,
1978): they "determined that this ratio (measured when knee extension torque is greatest)
should be nearer 80:20 for weightlifters and jumpers," while a treadmill-movement
measurement gives runners a ratio of approximately 50:50. A related popular belief, that
injuries are far more common once left/right lower-extremity strength differs by more than
10%, is also questioned. The authors cite "recent research" finding that neither
recommendation is supported by scientifically controlled experiments that correct torque
outputs for the effect of gravity and avoid stretching the hamstrings (Stephens & Reid,
1988). The flexor/extensor-ratio recommendation is additionally vague because the ratio
varies across the joint's range of motion. Verified against the page image (Fig 4.16, PDF p.
245, printed p. 234): the figure plots the ratio of isokinetic knee-extensor to knee-flexor
torque (y-axis 0.5 to 3.5) against joint angle at 36, 108 and 180 degrees/second, from
Cybex dynamometer data; the caption gives no source and no population, and states that

# Prepare Athletes for the Risky Movements Their Sport Contains Instead of Banning Them: Train Reaction, Anticipation and Falling

**What it is** — Under "Training to Avoid Injury" the authors write: "Avoidance of certain exercises which are regarded as potentially harmful may sometimes be unwise, because those very movements may occur periodically in the sport or during practice. This well-meaning approach can predispose athletes to injury since they will not have acquired the necessary involuntary motor skills to cope with higher risk actions. Therefore, it can be valuable to progressively introduce skills intended to prepare the athlete to minimise the chance of accidents and injury" (PDF 439 / p.428, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is skill: an athlete never exposed to a high-risk action lacks the "involuntary motor skills to cope" when the sport forces it. "Training of reactive ability can be extremely helpful in this regard, although too many athletes strengthen the body instead to achieve this end. It would be far better for them to improve speed of reaction, speed of movement, ability to anticipate impending dangers and to learn to manage dangerous events while they are happening" (PDF 439 / p.428).

**When to apply** — When a movement is dropped from a programme as "dangerous" but the sport still produces it (contact, falls, awkward landings). Introduce it "progressively." The authors' contact-sport case: "It is surprising how few rugby and American football players never learn how to fall from their colleagues in judo and wrestling, yet falling and violent bodily contact are integral parts of their games" (PDF 439 / p.428; the double negative "how few ... never" is printed so, and the sense is that few learn to fall). Eric's review: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the book's "progressively introduce" matches that rule; exposure is graded, not sudden.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors say avoidance "may sometimes be unwise," not always; a movement the sport does not contain is not covered. No injury data are given. "Too many athletes strengthen the body instead" sets reactive skill against strength, but the book does not say strength work is useless for injury risk. Inference: in a rehab or novice setting, holding back a high-risk movement until basic control is present is still graded exposure, not the avoidance the authors criticise.

**Example** — The authors' own: teaching rugby and American football players the falling skills used in judo and wrestling, since falling and contact are part of their games (PDF 439 / p.428).

**Related** — [[principle--return-to-play-incomplete-until-the-athlete-perceives-full-healing]], [[heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-only-unsafe-execution-for-individual]], [[claim--reaction-time-mostly-fixed-movement-time-trainable]], [[heuristic--progressive-and-random-segmental-training]]

**What it is** — It is often claimed the optimal quadriceps-to-hamstring strength ratio is

measurement gives runners a ratio of approximately 50:50. A related popular belief, that
injuries are far more common once left/right lower-extremity strength differs by more than
10%, is also questioned. The authors cite "recent research" finding that neither

- General rule for any test or technology, stated as a standing rule rather than a fresh call each time. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)**
- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- The dynamic strength index (DSI: CMJ against isometric mid-thigh pull peak force) chooses between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q21): "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** This is not the SJ-CMJ gap the question asked about. Evidence check done 2026-09-29 (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`): cite it as Eric's practice, tagged [contested; the ratio tracks IMTP strength; one controlled trial (Pleša 2024, basketball, split at 0.90) supported only the strength arm; no football data]. See Tension 17.
- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to claim injury prevention as achievable. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4; week1-lecture.md p.9]
- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice. Confirmed by the interview: there is no formal risk model.
- Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]), "the
difference between maximum strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and
absolute strength (involuntary effort) of which the athlete is capable in that same
action" (printed 9). True Fmm requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and
risky to test directly. As a field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from
a static, knees-flexed start (no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a
sudden dip (printed 9).

The book gives two different, conflicting rules for what a small versus large gap means.
The jump paragraph itself states: "If there
is a small difference between the two jumps, this suggests that training focuses more on
nervous stimulation via the use of 'shock' and ballistic methods such as plyometrics. If
the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM ... loads
using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable" (printed
9-10). The very next paragraph states the opposite pairing as a general rule: "In general,
if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength
may be produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via
weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be
induced by submaximal loading methods" (printed 10). These two statements directly
conflict on the jump test's own page: a small jump-test gap means shock/ballistic work by
the first statement and hypertrophy-then-heavy-loads by the second; a large gap means
5-8RM CAT strength/hypertrophy work by the first statement and weightlifting/plyometric
work by the second. No direction can be safely taken from this source alone. (PDF pp.
#####
**Related** — [[heuristic--heart-rate-work-capacity-tests-for-lifters]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[research-papers/thorpe-2017-monitoring-fatigue-status-in-elite-team-sport-athletes-implications-for-practice]], [[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]]
#####
**Related** — [[claim--collagen-loading-curve-and-injury-risk]]; [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]]; [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]; [[claim--squat-1-5-to-2-bodymass-rule-applies-to-maximal-depth-jumps-only]]

**Also in 8.2** — The same two classes reappear as "overload injuries (caused by too large a load at any instant) and overuse injuries (caused by very frequent application of a given load)," with an ordering rule: overload injuries from hard heel strike "may be diminished by the use of suitable footwear, but correction of technical faults and impact conditioning should take place first" (PDF 438 / p.427, checked against the page image). See [[framework--eight-types-of-needs-analysis]] (injury analysis).

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]), "the
difference between maximum strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and
absolute strength (involuntary effort) of which the athlete is capable in that same
action" (printed 9). True Fmm requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and
risky to test directly. As a field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from
a static, knees-flexed start (no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a
sudden dip (printed 9).

The book gives two different, conflicting rules for what a small versus large gap means.
The jump paragraph itself states: "If there
is a small difference between the two jumps, this suggests that training focuses more on
nervous stimulation via the use of 'shock' and ballistic methods such as plyometrics. If
the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM ... loads
using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable" (printed
9-10). The very next paragraph states the opposite pairing as a general rule: "In general,
if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength
may be produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via
weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be
induced by submaximal loading methods" (printed 10). These two statements directly
conflict on the jump test's own page: a small jump-test gap means shock/ballistic work by
the first statement and hypertrophy-then-heavy-loads by the second; a large gap means
5-8RM CAT strength/hypertrophy work by the first statement and weightlifting/plyometric
work by the second. No direction can be safely taken from this source alone. (PDF pp.
#####
**Related** — [[heuristic--heart-rate-work-capacity-tests-for-lifters]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]], [[research-papers/thorpe-2017-monitoring-fatigue-status-in-elite-team-sport-athletes-implications-for-practice]], [[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]]
#####
**Related** — [[claim--collagen-loading-curve-and-injury-risk]]; [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]]; [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]; [[claim--squat-1-5-to-2-bodymass-rule-applies-to-maximal-depth-jumps-only]]

**Also in 8.2** — The same two classes reappear as "overload injuries (caused by too large a load at any instant) and overuse injuries (caused by very frequent application of a given load)," with an ordering rule: overload injuries from hard heel strike "may be diminished by the use of suitable footwear, but correction of technical faults and impact conditioning should take place first" (PDF 438 / p.427, checked against the page image). See [[framework--eight-types-of-needs-analysis]] (injury analysis).

# McDougall's Four Values of Testing and Seven Characteristics of an Effective Testing Programme

**What it is** — Section 8.7 opens by restating that "the most specific test of all is performance in the actual sporting event. All other tests have varying degrees of correlation with performance or selected actions in the given sport" (PDF 468 / p.457, checked against the page image). The author, writing in the first person ("my Canadian colleague, Dr Duncan Mc Dougall"), then summarises McDougall et al (1982). Four values of "suitable, well-planned tests": (1) "They identify individual strengths and weaknesses and provide data for determining the baseline for training programmes"; (2) "They provide feedback on the effectiveness of training programmes"; (3) "They provide information on the athlete's state of health"; (4) "They provide an educational process which teaches the athlete to understand more competently his/her body and the demands of the sport." Seven characteristics of an effective programme: (1) "The variables which are tested must be directly relevant to the given sport"; (2) "The tests must be valid (test what it claims to), reliable and reproducible"; (3) "The testing procedures must be as sport specific as possible"; (4) "The testing situation must be rigidly controlled"; (5) "Testing must be repeated at regular, appropriate intervals"; (6) "The tests must respect the athlete's human rights (including ethics, confidentiality and risks)"; (7) "The results must be interpreted in understandable language directly to the athlete and coach" (PDF 468 / p.457). The author then says the section will not "reiterate what has already been written" by testing authorities and will "simply ... provide information which is not readily available" (PDF 468 / p.457). The book prints the name both as "Mc Dougall" and "McDougall"; the OCR's "Me Dougall" is an artifact.

**Why it works** — The book gives no separate mechanism; the lists rest on the opening point that every test other than competition is only a correlate of performance. Inference: items 1 and 3 keep that correlate as close to the sport as possible; items 2, 4 and 5 make a change between two test dates attributable to training rather than to noise or a changed protocol; item 7 makes the result usable by the people who change the programme.

**When to apply** — When building or auditing a test battery, or deciding whether to keep a test. Eric's review: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Eric's review: "Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 57, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's review: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 34, Explicit). Inference: McDougall's items 1, 4 and 5 match these lines; the baseline lines quoted here say nothing about item 6 (ethics and confidentiality) or item 7 (explaining results directly to the athlete).

**When NOT to apply** — The lists are a checklist, not evidence that testing improves results; McDougall et al (1982) is cited, not described, and `supported` rests on it being a named, standard text the author endorses. Inference: items 1 and 3 ("as sport specific as possible") pull against item 2 (reliability), since the most sport-like tests are often the hardest to control; Eric's own battery leans on general, reliable tests ("bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max", `docs/method-baseline.md`, line 58). The four values say what tests can "provide", not that every test must serve all four.

**Example** — The author applies item 3 at once to the vertical jump: because results "correlate best with conditions which are most similar to that of the test", it is "useful to repeat the test with the non-dominant hand or in the frontal plane with the athlete using both hands" (PDF 468 / p.457). See [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]].

**Related** — [[claim--laboratory-tests-cannot-predict-performance-or-select-talent]], [[heuristic--test-monthly-under-constant-conditions-and-compare-with-targets]] (constant conditions, monthly comparison, 6.16), [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]]

type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky

topic: limits of laboratory testing
category: [testing, talent-identification, selection, physiology]

ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-10-13

# Laboratory Tests Cannot Predict Performance or Pick Talent; Physiology Should Only Augment Performance Data in Selection

**What it is** — Three voices sit on this page. The author (first person) introduces McDougall's "remarks on the scope and limitations of testing, which so often tend to be ignored by sports scientists whose main role appears to be research publications rather than practical application of the data" (PDF 468 / p.457, checked against the page image). That jab is the author's. The quotation that follows is McDougall's (McDougall et al, 1982): "Laboratory testing is not a magical tool for predicting future gold medallists. It has severe limitations for identifying potential talent in that scientists still do not know how to determine 'genetic limits' and therefore cannot predict potential to improve. For example, the use of muscle biopsies to estimate muscle fiber types and thus predict endurance or power performance is highly questionable.... The complete performance of any athlete is a composite of many different factors of which physiological function is only one. It is therefore unwise to attempt to predict performance from any single physiological test or battery of physiological tests - especially in sports where technical, tactical, and psychological components may relegate physiology to a lesser role. Similarly, in the selection of athletes for competition or for teams, physiological tests should only augment information which is available on actual performances or field observations" (PDF 468 / p.457).

**Why it works** — McDougall's reasons are given in the quote: no method yet sets an individual's "genetic limits", and physiology is one factor among technical, tactical and psychological ones. Inference: a test that captures only one component of a composite cannot rank athletes on the composite, and the less physiology matters in a sport, the weaker that ranking gets.

**When to apply** — When a coach or administrator wants a test result to select, cut or project an athlete. The rule in the quote is concrete: performance and field observation lead, physiological tests "only augment". Inference: in team sports with large technical and tactical demands, treat a physiological battery as a check on the eye and the game record, not as the selector.

**When NOT to apply** — This is expert opinion from a 1982 text, quoted without data, so `untested`. The quote is about predicting future performance and selecting talent, not about the other uses of testing (baseline, feedback, health, education) that the same author lists on the same page; see [[framework--mcdougall-four-values-and-seven-characteristics-of-a-testing-programme]]. Inference: "scientists still do not know how to determine 'genetic limits'" and the biopsy example reflect the state of the field in 1982; they should be rechecked against current literature before being cited as current. The author's line about sports scientists chasing publications is a judgment with no evidence offered.

**Example** — McDougall's own: using "muscle biopsies to estimate muscle fiber types and thus predict endurance or power performance is highly questionable" (PDF 468 / p.457).

**Related** — [[framework--mcdougall-four-values-and-seven-characteristics-of-a-testing-programme]], [[case-study--vorobyev-vertical-jump-rises-with-weightlifter-qualification-table-8-13]]

# Vorobyev's Jerk Dip Parameters by Bar Weight (Table 8.12): Deeper, Longer Dips With Heavier Bars, Pause Never Over 0.25 s

**What it is** — Table 8.12, "Parameters of the Jerk Phase of the Olympic Clean-and-Jerk (Vorobyev, 1978)" (PDF 469 / p.458, every cell read from the page image):

| Weight of bar (kg) | Duration of dip (s) | Depth of dip (cm) | Duration of pause in dip (s) | Duration of jerk (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 120-140 | 0.15-0.20 | 5-8 | 0.00-0.15 | 0.15-0.20 |
| 160-180 | 0.20-0.30 | 8-10 | 0.00-0.20 | 0.20-0.25 |
| 200-220 | 0.40-0.50 | 10-15 | 0.00-0.25 | 0.25-0.35 |

The book reads it as showing "that the dip characteristically is deeper for heavier loads or persons and that in all cases the pause during the dip should not last longer than 0.25 second" (PDF 469 / p.458; "the dip" and "should not" are on the compressed right margin, partly reconstructed). It draws a training use: "Herein lies the benefit of performing push jerks or jerks off racks with different weights as a form of supplementary plyometric training. After all, plyometric training is of little value if it fails to enhance adequately explosive strength or power over the range required in a given activity. The use of drills which do not correlate strongly with the functional needs of a given sport constitute one of the most common errors in popular plyometric training" (PDF 469 / p.458, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "different", "if it fails", "use of drills", "common"). Two caveats follow: the measurements used "an Olympic weightlifting bar, so that the values of the parameters during the pause and jerk phase will be different for other training bars," and "optimal interaction between bar and lifter occurs when the frequency of oscillation of the bar is twice that of the lifter's movement (Vorobyev, 1978)" (PDF 469 / p.458).

**Why it works** — The book's logic: the jerk dip is a short eccentric-concentric reversal under load, so loading it at several weights trains rebound over the range a lifter actually uses. Inference: the 0.25 s ceiling on the pause is the same idea as keeping the amortization phase short so stored elastic energy is not lost (see [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]]); the book does not make that link on this page.

**When to apply** — When choosing a loaded plyometric for an athlete whose sport needs explosive leg drive over a short dip, or when coaching the jerk: keep the pause in the dip brief. Inference: push jerks or jerks from racks at varied weights are the book's suggested means; how much they transfer outside weightlifting is not tested here.

**When NOT to apply** — The data are from weightlifters handling 120-220 kg, with no sample size, lifter bodymass or class given; the "or persons" part of the reading is not in the table, which lists bar weight only. Values apply to an Olympic bar, as the book itself warns. The bar-oscillation rule is stated without method or data. Inference: for team-sport athletes jerking far lighter loads, the dip depths and times in the table are not targets.

**Example** — At 200-220 kg the dip lasts 0.40-0.50 s and goes 10-15 cm deep, against 0.15-0.20 s and 5-8 cm at 120-140 kg; the pause stays at 0.25 s or less in every row (PDF 469 / p.458).

**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], [[case-study--vorobyev-vertical-jump-rises-with-weightlifter-qualification-table-8-13]], [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]]

# Vorobyev's Jerk Dip Parameters by Bar Weight (Table 8.12): Deeper, Longer Dips With Heavier Bars, Pause Never Over 0.25 s

**What it is** — Table 8.12, "Parameters of the Jerk Phase of the Olympic Clean-and-Jerk (Vorobyev, 1978)" (PDF 469 / p.458, every cell read from the page image):

| Weight of bar (kg) | Duration of dip (s) | Depth of dip (cm) | Duration of pause in dip (s) | Duration of jerk (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 120-140 | 0.15-0.20 | 5-8 | 0.00-0.15 | 0.15-0.20 |
| 160-180 | 0.20-0.30 | 8-10 | 0.00-0.20 | 0.20-0.25 |
| 200-220 | 0.40-0.50 | 10-15 | 0.00-0.25 | 0.25-0.35 |

The book reads it as showing "that the dip characteristically is deeper for heavier loads or persons and that in all cases the pause during the dip should not last longer than 0.25 second" (PDF 469 / p.458; "the dip" and "should not" are on the compressed right margin, partly reconstructed). It draws a training use: "Herein lies the benefit of performing push jerks or jerks off racks with different weights as a form of supplementary plyometric training. After all, plyometric training is of little value if it fails to enhance adequately explosive strength or power over the range required in a given activity. The use of drills which do not correlate strongly with the functional needs of a given sport constitute one of the most common errors in popular plyometric training" (PDF 469 / p.458, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "different", "if it fails", "use of drills", "common"). Two caveats follow: the measurements used "an Olympic weightlifting bar, so that the values of the parameters during the pause and jerk phase will be different for other training bars," and "optimal interaction between bar and lifter occurs when the frequency of oscillation of the bar is twice that of the lifter's movement (Vorobyev, 1978)" (PDF 469 / p.458).

**Why it works** — The book's logic: the jerk dip is a short eccentric-concentric reversal under load, so loading it at several weights trains rebound over the range a lifter actually uses. Inference: the 0.25 s ceiling on the pause is the same idea as keeping the amortization phase short so stored elastic energy is not lost (see [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]]); the book does not make that link on this page.

**When to apply** — When choosing a loaded plyometric for an athlete whose sport needs explosive leg drive over a short dip, or when coaching the jerk: keep the pause in the dip brief. Inference: push jerks or jerks from racks at varied weights are the book's suggested means; how much they transfer outside weightlifting is not tested here.

**When NOT to apply** — The data are from weightlifters handling 120-220 kg, with no sample size, lifter bodymass or class given; the "or persons" part of the reading is not in the table, which lists bar weight only. Values apply to an Olympic bar, as the book itself warns. The bar-oscillation rule is stated without method or data. Inference: for team-sport athletes jerking far lighter loads, the dip depths and times in the table are not targets.

**Example** — At 200-220 kg the dip lasts 0.40-0.50 s and goes 10-15 cm deep, against 0.15-0.20 s and 5-8 cm at 120-140 kg; the pause stays at 0.25 s or less in every row (PDF 469 / p.458).

**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], [[case-study--vorobyev-vertical-jump-rises-with-weightlifter-qualification-table-8-13]], [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]]

# Vertical Jump Rises With Weightlifting Qualification: 57.3 cm in Novices to 85.5 cm in Elite (Table 8.13)

**What it is** — Table 8.13, "Mean dynamic start Vertical Jump for Olympic Weightlifters from all divisions (Vorobyev, 1978)" (PDF 469 / p.458, every cell read from the page image): Novice 57.3 cm; Class III 58.1; Class II 65.3; Class I 67.8; Master of Sport 72.3; Elite 85.5. The book offers these as "Guidelines concerning the vertical jump height for different levels of competitive weightlifter." It adds two individual results it calls "noteworthy": a former high-jump world-record holder with a best vertical jump of 102 cm, and a superheavyweight champion weightlifter who reached 91 cm "despite his enormous bodymass (over 140kg)." Its reading: "these competitors displayed exceptional absolute vertical jumps, as well as excellent relative vertical jumps (height per unit bodymass) and leg power" (PDF 469 / p.458, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "high jump", "champion", "vertical"). The two athletes are named in the book; the names are not carried here.

**Why it works** — The book gives no mechanism. Inference: the weightlifting classes are ranked by lifted totals that depend on explosive leg extension, so a rising jump with class is what one would expect if the jump and the lifts share that quality; the table is cross-sectional, so it shows association, not that training raised the jump.

**When to apply** — As a rough reference when testing weightlifters with a dynamic-start jump (the book's condition 4 or 5 in [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]]). Inference: the biggest step is from Master of Sport to Elite (13.2 cm), while Novice to Class III differs by only 0.8 cm, so the jump separates the top of the sport far better than the bottom.

**When NOT to apply** — Means only, with no spread, sample size or test details beyond "dynamic start"; whether arms were used is not stated. Weightlifters "from all divisions" are pooled, so heavy and light lifters sit in one mean, and the book's own point is that relative jump (per bodymass) matters. Inference: these 1978 Soviet norms are not norms for team-sport athletes or for force-plate jump height, which is computed differently from a reach test.

**Example** — Elite weightlifters averaged 85.5 cm against 72.3 cm for Masters of Sport (PDF 469 / p.458).

**Related** — [[claim--vorobyev-mean-training-weight-by-bodymass-and-qualification]] (Vorobyev's by-class training data), [[case-study--vorobyev-jerk-dip-parameters-by-bar-weight-table-8-12]], [[claim--laboratory-tests-cannot-predict-performance-or-select-talent]]

# Weightlifters' Extensors Are About 2.9 Times Stronger Than Their Flexors, Far From the 1.5 "Norm"

**What it is** — Under "Muscle Strength Ratios" the book takes on "the most commonly quoted" agonist-antagonist ratio, "the 60:40 ratio of knee extension to knee flexion strength (i.e. extensors 1.5 times stronger than flexors)," and refers back to Section 4.2.6.2 for its limitations (PDF 469 / p.458, checked against the page image). It adds that "these ratios not only vary with joint angle, joint velocity and type of movement, but also with muscle group and the type of athlete." Its data (Vorobyev, 1978): "the relative isometric strength (per 1kg bodymass) of the larger extensor muscles in Olympic weightlifters is 11.51 ± 1.78, and for the major flexors it is 4.02 ± 0.69 ... In general, their major extensors are on average 2.86 times stronger than their major flexors, a figure which is very different from the isokinetic value of 1.5 cited by sports physiotherapists for the average person (whatever this entity might be)" (PDF 469-470 / pp.458-459; "In general" and "different" sit on the compressed right margin of PDF 469 and are partly reconstructed). By region, "Among the best Russian weightlifters the relative maximum strength of extensors to flexors is as follows: arms 1.6:1, trunk 4.3:1, thighs 4.3:1, and lower leg 5.4:1" (PDF 470 / p.459). The conclusion: "The application of these findings on their own to sport or rehabilitation is incomplete and must be accompanied by the profile of strength produced at important joint angles in every given sport, in accordance with the principle of dynamic correspondence, especially the accentuated region of force production (Section 4.3)" (PDF 470 / p.459).

**Why it works** — The book's reasoning is specificity: a ratio reflects the muscles a sport loads, so an athlete whose sport is dominated by extension will show high extensor-to-flexor ratios without being "imbalanced." Inference: 11.51 / 4.02 = 2.86, so the book's "2.86 times" is the ratio of the two group means.

**When to apply** — Before calling an athlete "imbalanced" from a ratio: check which athlete type, muscle group, joint angle, speed and contraction type the reference ratio came from. Then, as the book says, pair the ratio with the strength profile at the joint angles the sport uses (see [[heuristic--train-force-at-the-accentuated-joint-angle]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The 2.86 figure is isometric and for weightlifters; the 1.5 it is set against is isokinetic and for "the average person," so the book compares two different measures, which is part of its point. Inference: the 4.2.6.2 entry reports Vorobyev's isokinetic knee ratio of "nearer 80:20 for weightlifters" ([[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]]); 80:20 is 4:1, close to the thigh ratio of 4.3:1 here, and different in kind from the whole-body 2.86. These are different measurements, not a conflict, so not `contested`. No sample sizes, test positions or "larger extensor" and "major flexor" muscle lists are given. Weightlifter ratios are not targets for other sports.

**Example** — The lower leg shows the most extreme ratio among the best Russian weightlifters, 5.4:1, against 1.6:1 for the arms (PDF 470 / p.459).

**Related** — [[heuristic--isokinetic-strength-ratios-vary-by-angle-and-velocity]], [[heuristic--train-force-at-the-accentuated-joint-angle]]

# The Shtanga Functional Pressure Test: Blood Pressure After a Forced Breath-Hold as an Overtraining Check in Weightlifters (Ulchenko)

**What it is** — Under "Work Capacity and Functional Pressure Tests," which the book calls "an extension" of the Ch 6.2.2 tests, it describes "the cardiac function Shtanga Functional Pressure test to ascertain if the athlete is overtraining (described by Vyurberg, 1953)," regarded as "particularly suitable for athletes like Olympic weightlifters and wrestlers, whose sports require them to strain against heavy resistance" (PDF 470 / p.459, checked against the page image). Procedure: breathe in relaxed fashion for a few minutes, inhale maximally, hold "for 15-20 seconds before stopping the nose and exhaling as forcibly as possible for 2 seconds," which brings "a sharp rise in intrathoracic pressure and diminished flow of blood to the heart." Blood pressure is taken before (BP1), immediately after (BP2) and after 2 minutes of relaxed breathing (BP3). "If the contractile processes of the myocardium are normal, as in the well-prepared athlete who is not exhibiting chronic fatigue, the blood pressure decreases briefly by 5-10mm Hg." Ulchenko (1982) used it "among elite weightlifters during their specific preparation stage": Test 1, the three readings before training; Test 2, the same readings "during the most intense training loading." Grades: "1. BP decrease after Test 1 or no change after Test 2. This is regarded as an excellent reaction. 2. BP increase of up to 5mm Hg immediately after Test 2 and recovery of normal BP after 2 minutes rest. This is considered to be a good reaction. 3. BP increase of up to 7mm Hg after Test 2 and 5 minutes recovery time. This is regarded as satisfactory. 4. BP increase of 10mm Hg or more after Test 2 and prolonged elevation of BP afterwards. This is regarded as an unsatisfactory response and is associated with an overtraining state" (PDF 470 / p.459). One lifter who "reported feeling fit and strong" with low RPE scored: Test 1, BP1 130/70, BP2 140/75, BP3 135/70, a 10 mm rise "regarded as unsatisfactory"; Test 2, BP1 140/66, BP2 160/70, BP3 142/70, a 20 mm rise, also unsatisfactory. "This lifter and several others whose pressure tests were deemed to be unacceptable did not improve their results in the competition which followed," and their coaches were advised to modify training "until the pressure tests indicated a better functional state" (PDF 470 / p.459). Ulchenko "strongly advised the regular application of this pressure test," even "as an almost daily routine," and "stated that the underlying cause of this diminished functional state is certainly due to weakening of the heart's contractile ability" (PDF 471 / p.460, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "of this", "work", "weakening of", "routine to").

**Why it works** — Ulchenko's reasoning as reported: strength sports involve "straining, breath-holding and high nervous tension which, in the presence of even small disturbances in functioning of the cardiovascular system, can aggravate the situation" (PDF 470-471 / pp.459-460), and a heart with weakened contractility handles the pressure challenge worse. Inference: the rises quoted are systolic (130 to 140, 140 to 160); diastolic barely moves.

**When to apply** — The book's case: heavy strength or grappling athletes in a hard preparation block, when self-report looks fine but results stall. Read with [[principle--pair-objective-and-subjective-tests-because-rpe-can-miss-a-poor-functional-state]], which draws the book's general lesson from the same lifter.

**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: the method is described, but no sample size, comparison group or statistics are given, and the competition outcome is "this lifter and several others." Inference: a cardiovascular stress test belongs with medical staff, not as a coach-run daily screen.

**Example** — The anonymous lifter above: low RPE on clean pulls and back squats, a 20 mm systolic rise under peak loading, and no improvement at the next competition (PDF 470 / p.459).

# Use Objective and Subjective Tests Together: an Athlete's RPE Can Look Fine While the Functional State Is Poor

**What it is** — The book draws a general lesson from one lifter in Ulchenko's study: he "reported feeling fit and strong and his RPE (Rating of Perceived Effort) was low during non-maximal loads (with exercises including clean pulls and back squats), but the Shtanga Test revealed that the actual functional state of the lifter was below par" (PDF 470 / p.459, checked against the page image). The lesson: "It is noteworthy that subjective assessments by the athlete (including RPE) did not accurately reveal his functional state, which emphasizes the importance of administering both objective and subjective tests (see Ch 6.2.2), especially if one wishes to ensure the appropriateness of a given periodisation scheme for any athlete" (PDF 471 / p.460; "his" and "(see Ch" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed).

**Why it works** — The book does not explain why the athlete's perception missed it. Inference: RPE here was rated on non-maximal loads, where a lifter can feel strong while a system the loads do not tax is already struggling; an objective probe of that system catches what the effort rating cannot.

**When to apply** — When a periodisation scheme is being steered mostly by how the athlete feels, add at least one objective marker. Eric's review: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Eric's review: "Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89, Explicit). Inference: the book asks for both kinds of test, not objective in place of subjective; Eric's practice is objective-first for the roster and both for return-to-play and chronic conditions, which is closer to the book in those groups. RPE on the session is not the same tool as a wellness survey, and the baseline lines quoted do not say whether session RPE is kept.

**When NOT to apply** — One athlete, so `untested`. The objective test in the case has its own printed inconsistencies ([[case-study--shtanga-functional-pressure-test-ulchenko-weightlifters]]), so the case shows a disagreement between two measures, and the competition result is the only sign of which one was right. The book does not say subjective measures are useless; it says they did not reveal this athlete's state.

**Example** — Low RPE on clean pulls and back squats alongside an "unsatisfactory" pressure test, followed by no improvement in competition (PDF 470 / p.459).

**Related** — [[case-study--shtanga-functional-pressure-test-ulchenko-weightlifters]], [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]] (the Ch 6.2.2 RPE material the text points back to), [[framework--butterfly-catastrophe-model-of-exercise-imbalance-injury-fig-8-9]] (objective and subjective tests to find an athlete's path)

# "No Dangerous Exercise, Only a Dangerous Way of Doing It": the Rule and the Eight Facts That Limit It

**What it is** — Section 8.8 restates an earlier rule and then qualifies it: "At the very outset, let us reiterate what has been said before: There is no such thing as a dangerous exercise .... There is only a dangerous way of doing any exercise. Is this a valid general rule? While it is very often true, we also have to note that:" (PDF 471 / p.460, checked against the page image; "exercise" and "true" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). The eight qualifications: "Injury is often a cumulative process"; "The most recent exercise or activity can be the final trigger"; "Injuries may be the result of "too much, too soon" of a safe thing (overtraining)"; "Injuries may be caused by inadequate pre-exercise preparation ("warm-up")"; "Accidents happen"; "Cause and effect are not linearly related"; "Individual responses to exercise are different"; "Injuries are context or situation dependent" (PDF 471 / p.460). Later the authors add that "Many manoeuvres which necessitate a high degree of skill or courage should undoubtedly be labelled as intrinsically dangerous for the average person, but not for the expert performer. There are safe and dangerous ways of executing virtually every human movement, including sitting, standing and walking" (PDF 472 / p.461). On PDF 477 they restate it: "the lack of safety in exercise is not simply a consequence of so-called dangerous exercises, but also one of unsafe execution of any exercise. Exercise safety must always be viewed in the context of the overall training session or programme for each specific individual" (PDF 477 / p.466, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "lack of", "execution of", "programme").

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: risk is a property of the exercise, the person, their state and the whole programme together. "While certain exercises may be intrinsically less safe for the relative novice to training, they may pose minimal risks for the same person after several months of training. Conversely, the least demanding and simplest of exercises may cause serious injury to an elite athlete who is careless, unmotivated or overtrained" (PDF 477 / p.466). The section closes: "exercise safety is largely a consequence of skill development (neuromuscular efficiency) and may be enhanced by imposing activities which progress carefully with respect to factors such as complexity, intensity, volume, speed, range of movement, duration, variety, level of fatigue and mental state" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**When to apply** — When someone wants an exercise banned as "dangerous": ask for whom, in what state, at what dose and inside what programme. For beginners the authors still say "it is undoubtedly preferable to err on the side of conservatism," while warning that "religious avoidance of certain exercises can lead to an overall imbalance between muscle groups or in motor coordination and increase the likelihood of injury during the sports event. Furthermore, the avoidance of exercising a muscle group in a particular way never enhances safety; it simply weakens those muscles relative to the exercise pattern which is avoided" (PDF 477 / p.466). Eric's review: "safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41, Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)). Inference: that is the authors' "err on the side of conservatism" for beginners, paired with their progression rule rather than a ban.

**When NOT to apply** — The rule is the authors' position, not a tested finding; no injury data are given, so `untested`.
