# Six Fundamental Principles of the Injury Process: Injury Can Be Minimised, Not Entirely Prevented

**What it is** — Section 8.8 opens by setting the scope of safety: programme design "would be incomplete without serious attention being paid to all aspects of safety in training, including safety of the means and methods of training, the individual exercises, the combination of exercises, the intensity, the volume of exercise, the timing of training loads, and the recovery periods (between repetitions, sets and sessions). An otherwise carefully-devised training programme is of little value if it causes injury to the athlete" (PDF 471 / p.460, checked against the page image; "combination", "(between" and "causes" are on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). Injuries come from "accident or overtraining." Accidents often depend on factors "outside the direct control of the athlete," yet "thorough physical preparation, astute situation analysis, training of reactive ability, efficient ongoing interpretation of feedback from cues provided by other players or the environment, and good anticipation can prove invaluable in minimising the risks" (PDF 471 / p.460). From the qualifications to the "no dangerous exercise" rule, the authors state "some fundamental principles of the injury process": "Injuries are not necessarily determinate, predictable and preventable"; "Causes of acute traumatic injury are more readily identifiable"; "Causes of insidious injury are much more hypothetical"; "Injury can be minimised, but not entirely prevented"; "Injury and Adaptation are both the result of stress. No stress - no progress - no injury !"; "There is no sharp zone of distinction between safety and danger, balance and imbalance" (PDF 471 / p.460).

**Why it works** — The authors derive the principles from the qualifications just listed: injury is cumulative, nonlinear, individual and context dependent ([[framework--no-dangerous-exercises-rule-and-its-eight-qualifications]]). Inference: if cause and effect are not linear and the last session may only be the trigger, then a single cause cannot be reliably named for insidious injuries, and risk can be shifted but not removed.

**When to apply** — When setting expectations with coaches and administrators about what an injury-prevention programme can promise, and when reviewing an injury: acute traumatic causes can be looked for; insidious causes are hypotheses. Eric's review: "Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to claim injury prevention as achievable." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 140, Inferred (transcript + slides); the em dash is in the baseline). Inference: the authors' "Injury can be minimised, but not entirely prevented" is the same position.

**When NOT to apply** — These are stated principles with no data, so `untested`. "No stress - no progress - no injury" does not say all stress is equally useful; the dose question is handled in [[principle--find-the-optimum-stress-level-rather-than-avoiding-stress]]. Inference: "not necessarily ... preventable" is not a reason to stop tracking load; the same section says overtraining "may be avoided" by planning, recording and monitoring volume and intensity (PDF 473 / p.462).

**Example** — The authors' contrast: the cause of an acute traumatic injury such as a collision is "more readily identifiable" than the cause of an insidious one, which is "much more hypothetical" (PDF 471 / p.460).

# Six Fundamental Principles of the Injury Process: Injury Can Be Minimised, Not Entirely Prevented

**What it is** — Section 8.8 opens by setting the scope of safety: programme design "would be incomplete without serious attention being paid to all aspects of safety in training, including safety of the means and methods of training, the individual exercises, the combination of exercises, the intensity, the volume of exercise, the timing of training loads, and the recovery periods (between repetitions, sets and sessions). An otherwise carefully-devised training programme is of little value if it causes injury to the athlete" (PDF 471 / p.460, checked against the page image; "combination", "(between" and "causes" are on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). Injuries come from "accident or overtraining." Accidents often depend on factors "outside the direct control of the athlete," yet "thorough physical preparation, astute situation analysis, training of reactive ability, efficient ongoing interpretation of feedback from cues provided by other players or the environment, and good anticipation can prove invaluable in minimising the risks" (PDF 471 / p.460). From the qualifications to the "no dangerous exercise" rule, the authors state "some fundamental principles of the injury process": "Injuries are not necessarily determinate, predictable and preventable"; "Causes of acute traumatic injury are more readily identifiable"; "Causes of insidious injury are much more hypothetical"; "Injury can be minimised, but not entirely prevented"; "Injury and Adaptation are both the result of stress. No stress - no progress - no injury !"; "There is no sharp zone of distinction between safety and danger, balance and imbalance" (PDF 471 / p.460).

**Why it works** — The authors derive the principles from the qualifications just listed: injury is cumulative, nonlinear, individual and context dependent ([[framework--no-dangerous-exercises-rule-and-its-eight-qualifications]]). Inference: if cause and effect are not linear and the last session may only be the trigger, then a single cause cannot be reliably named for insidious injuries, and risk can be shifted but not removed.

**When to apply** — When setting expectations with coaches and administrators about what an injury-prevention programme can promise, and when reviewing an injury: acute traumatic causes can be looked for; insidious causes are hypotheses. Eric's review: "Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 140, Inferred (transcript + slides); the line continues that this is "an explicit refusal to claim injury prevention as achievable"). Inference: the authors' "Injury can be minimised, but not entirely prevented" is the same position.

**When NOT to apply** — These are stated principles with no data, so `untested`. "No stress - no progress - no injury" does not say all stress is equally useful; the dose question is handled in [[principle--find-the-optimum-stress-level-rather-than-avoiding-stress]]. Inference: "not necessarily ... preventable" is not a reason to stop tracking load; the same section says overtraining "may be avoided" by planning, recording and monitoring volume and intensity (PDF 473 / p.462).

**Example** — The authors' contrast: the cause of an acute traumatic injury such as a collision is "more readily identifiable" than the cause of an insidious one, which is "much more hypothetical" (PDF 471 / p.460).

**Related** — [[framework--no-dangerous-exercises-rule-and-its-eight-qualifications]], [[claim--undertraining-is-not-safe-and-maximum-tolerable-load-is-not-the-optimum]], [[framework--butterfly-catastrophe-model-of-exercise-imbalance-injury-fig-8-9]]

# Undertraining Is Not Safe, and the Most Load an Athlete Can Survive Is Not the Optimum

**What it is** — The authors reject two opposite errors. First, the old belief of "the more training the better" or "no gain without pain," imposed "on misguided athletes either by themselves or by uninformed coaches, since they maintain that the optimum training load is the maximum training load a person can endure without injury" (PDF 471 / p.460, checked against the page image; "often", "or by" and "person can" are on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). "More enlightened coaches" keep the principle but start "at low intensity and continually increase intensity and duration within individual limits of endurance and the time available" (PDF 471-472 / pp.460-461). Second, the opposite belief: "It would then possibly appear as if overtraining is the sole cause of non-accidental training injuries, whereas undertraining is safe and merely leads to lack of progress. This is only partly true. Consistent undertraining, which never familiarizes the athlete with high stress levels or the so-called 'pain-barrier', may expose him to risk during the excitement of a competition. Moreover, undertraining accompanied by faulty technique, drug usage, inadequate sleep, poor nutrition or the use of unsuitable equipment can also lead to injury" (PDF 472 / p.461; the first letters of "undertraining", "which", "during" and "inadequate" are cut by the left margin and are partly reconstructed). The six injury principles on the previous page compress the point: "No stress - no progress - no injury !" (PDF 471 / p.460).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is unfamiliarity: an athlete never exposed in training to the stress levels of competition meets them for the first time when the stakes and arousal are highest. Inference: this is the injury-side version of the book's adaptation argument, where avoiding stress leaves the athlete less able to cope with it.

**When to apply** — When a cautious programme keeps training loads well under what competition demands "to stay safe." Eric's review: "Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 40, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's review: "Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 88, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors and the baseline make the same argument; the authors add that it is an injury risk, not only a performance cost.

**When NOT to apply** — No injury data are given, so `untested`. In the second sentence the named risks (faulty technique, drugs, poor sleep, poor nutrition, unsuitable equipment) do the injuring; undertraining only accompanies them. Inference: the claim does not license loading past an athlete's current limits; the authors' own fix is the "enlightened" gradual increase "within individual limits." The "pain-barrier" phrase is not defined.

**Example** — The authors' case: an athlete who has trained consistently below competition stress "may" be exposed to risk "during the excitement of a competition" (PDF 472 / p.461).

**Related** — [[principle--find-the-optimum-stress-level-rather-than-avoiding-stress]] (8.5), [[framework--six-fundamental-principles-of-the-injury-process]], [[claim--overtraining-injury-parallels-engineering-fatigue-from-overload-and-overuse]]

# Overtraining Injury Is Real: It Parallels Engineering Failure From Overload and From Overuse (Metal Fatigue)

**What it is** — The authors report a view they reject. Some coaches "believe that lack of suppleness is the major non-traumatic cause of injuries. They, together with several medical experts, assert that there is no clinical condition identifiable as overtraining and that the term 'overtraining injury' more precisely should be applied to damage caused by lack of suppleness, faulty technique, inappropriate footwear and so on" (PDF 472 / p.461, checked against the page image; the left margin cuts "available", "non-traumatic", "condition" and "damage", partly reconstructed). Their answer: overtraining "classically is categorised as follows: overload (too large a load at any given instant - "too heavy") and overuse (too large a quantity of work or exercise - "too much")," and "The fact remains that the equivalent of overtraining and overtraining injuries is well known in physics and engineering, under much the same categories" (PDF 472 / p.461). Large forces from "either large masses or large accelerations" (Force = Mass x Acceleration) "can lead to rapid failure of any mechanical system," and "The frequent application of moderate forces or the occasional application of large, impulsive forces can cause metal fatigue, structural failure or general deterioration of some or many of the components of a system." The body differs in that it "performs a great deal, but not all, of its own repair (most of it during periods of what we call passive or active "rest", "restoration" or "recuperation")," yet "it is clear that structural weakening or failure of an engineering system has its parallel in the human body, whether it be called 'overtraining injury', 'overuse injury' or something else" (PDF 472 / p.461).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the engineering one: material fails either from one load beyond its strength or from repeated loads below it that accumulate damage. Inference: the body's repair between loads is the difference from a machine; when repair keeps pace, repeated loading is training, and when it does not, it is fatigue damage.

**When to apply** — When a coach or clinician blames every non-contact injury on flexibility, technique or shoes: the load history (too heavy at an instant, or too much over time) is a cause in its own right. The authors' practical rule: "Overtraining is entirely controllable by the athlete and may be avoided" by planning, recording and monitoring "the volume (repetitions, sets and rest periods in resistance training; duration and distance in running and other cyclic activities) and intensity (maximum weight used; time or speed in running, etc.)" (PDF 473 / p.462, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "may be", "volume", "cyclic").

**When NOT to apply** — An analogy, not data, so `untested`. Inference: "entirely controllable by the athlete" sits uneasily beside the same section's "Injuries are not necessarily determinate, predictable and preventable" (PDF 471 / p.460); the two are about overtraining and injury respectively, so this is a tension in emphasis, not the same claim contradicted, and the entry is not marked `contested`. On PDF 472 the authors write "As we shall learn in more detail later" before the overload and overuse definitions, while PDF 473 says "we noted in the previous section" the acute (overreaching) and chronic (overtraining) distinction; both point to other parts of the book.

**Example** — The authors' engineering case: cars, machines and structures "require regular inspection and maintenance" because frequent moderate forces or occasional large impulsive ones cause fatigue failure (PDF 472 / p.461).

**Related** — [[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]] (overload and overuse in 5.2.4 and 8.2), [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]] (the acute and chronic distinction), [[claim--undertraining-is-not-safe-and-maximum-tolerable-load-is-not-the-optimum]], [[claim--stiffer-tissue-reaches-its-elastic-limit-sooner-for-the-same-energy-fig-8-8]]

# Undertraining Is Not Safe, and the Most Load an Athlete Can Survive Is Not the Optimum

**What it is** — The authors reject two opposite errors. First, the old belief of "the more training the better" or "no gain without pain," imposed "on misguided athletes either by themselves or by uninformed coaches, since they maintain that the optimum training load is the maximum training load a person can endure without injury" (PDF 471 / p.460, checked against the page image; "often", "or by" and "person can" are on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). "More enlightened coaches" keep the principle but start "at low intensity and continually increase intensity and duration within individual limits of endurance and the time available" (PDF 471-472 / pp.460-461). Second, the opposite belief: "It would then possibly appear as if overtraining is the sole cause of non-accidental training injuries, whereas undertraining is safe and merely leads to lack of progress. This is only partly true. Consistent undertraining, which never familiarizes the athlete with high stress levels or the so-called 'pain-barrier', may expose him to risk during the excitement of a competition. Moreover, undertraining accompanied by faulty technique, drug usage, inadequate sleep, poor nutrition or the use of unsuitable equipment can also lead to injury" (PDF 472 / p.461; the first letters of "undertraining", "which", "during" and "inadequate" are cut by the left margin and are partly reconstructed). The six injury principles on the previous page compress the point: "No stress - no progress - no injury !" (PDF 471 / p.460).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is unfamiliarity: an athlete never exposed in training to the stress levels of competition meets them for the first time when the stakes and arousal are highest. Inference: this is the injury-side version of the book's adaptation argument, where avoiding stress leaves the athlete less able to cope with it.

**When to apply** — When a cautious programme keeps training loads well under what competition demands "to stay safe." Eric's review: "Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 40, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's review: "Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 88, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors and the baseline make the same argument; the authors add that it is an injury risk, not only a performance cost.

**When NOT to apply** — No injury data are given, so `untested`. In the second sentence the named risks (faulty technique, drugs, poor sleep, poor nutrition, unsuitable equipment) do the injuring; undertraining only accompanies them. Inference: the claim does not license loading past an athlete's current limits; the authors' own fix is the "enlightened" gradual increase "within individual limits." The "pain-barrier" phrase is not defined.

**Example** — The authors' case: an athlete who has trained consistently below competition stress "may" be exposed to risk "during the excitement of a competition" (PDF 472 / p.461).

# Four Categories of Exercise by Stress and Structural Integrity (Fig 8.6): Stay in Category A Except to Overload Progressively

**What it is** — "If one considers the type of stress and the integrity of the body structure involved, a useful categorization of exercise emerges (Fig 8.6)" (PDF 472 / p.461, checked against the page image). Fig 8.6, "Classification of exercises in terms of levels of stress (Siff, 1984)," is a 2 x 2 grid read from the image: columns are Exercise Stress (normal, abnormal), rows are Integrity of Bodily Structures (normal, abnormal). A = normal stress on a normal structure; B = abnormal stress on a normal structure; C = normal stress on an abnormal structure; D = abnormal stress on an abnormal structure. Definitions: "'Normality' is always a relative expression and here it applies at a specific time to the individual, whose structure imposes a certain range of efficient, injury-free operation. 'Abnormal' stress in this context refers generally to loading of excessive duration, magnitude or inappropriate movement pattern, where 'excessive' refers to loading that is at or beyond certain limits of the athlete's current level of structural or functional adaptation. A structure of 'abnormal' integrity is one which is unprepared, injured, diseased, genetically unsound, fatigued, or generally impaired in structure or function at a given time (Siff, 1984)" (PDF 472-473 / pp.461-462). The rule: "Safety of exercise can be considerably enhanced if one ensures that activity very rarely falls outside category A, except to permit astute application of the principle of gradual progressive overload (Fig 8.6). This entails a thorough familiarity with general principles of kinesiology and the specific capabilities of the individual at any given time" (PDF 473 / p.462; "category", "entails a" and "at any" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). The section then "focuses largely on category B exercise (abnormal stress on normal structures) encountered in non-contact sports, mainly because this is the most frequently underestimated type of unsafe exercise" (PDF 473 / p.462).

**Why it works** — Both axes are defined relative to the individual "at a given time," so the same session can be category A for one athlete and B or D for another, or for the same athlete when fatigued. Inference: progressive overload has to step briefly past the current limit to drive adaptation, which is why the rule allows excursions out of A only for that purpose.

**When to apply** — As a quick screen when planning a session or a return-to-training step: is the load within this athlete's current adaptation (column), and is the tissue ready today (row)? Inference: category C (normal stress on an impaired structure) is the everyday case in return to play and in heavily fatigued athletes, where a load that is routine for teammates is excessive for this one.

**When NOT to apply** — A classification, not a measured model; "normal" and "abnormal" are the authors' own placeholder terms ("For want of more descriptive terms"), and the book gives no way to measure where the boundary sits, so `untested`. Inference: because "abnormal" is defined as "at or beyond certain limits of the athlete's current level of ... adaptation," the grid cannot be applied without some estimate of that limit, which is exactly the hard part.

**Example** — The authors' focus case: category B, abnormal stress on normal structures in non-contact sports, which they call "the most frequently underestimated type of unsafe exercise" (PDF 473 / p.462).

# Injury Proneness and the Stability-Mobility Balance: Six Factors Link the Two (Fig 8.7)

**What it is** — Under "Biomechanical Models of the Injury Process" the authors say individual injury proneness "is not always appreciated by athletes and their coaches, largely because genetic or structural susceptibility to damage is not easy to measure." It "depends on a variety of factors including inherent muscle, tendon and ligament strength and mechanical stiffness (not the same as the "stiffness" relating to limitation in range of movement); the ratio of 'functional' force/torque production between so-called 'agonistic' and 'antagonistic' muscles; limb leverages; and previous injury" (PDF 473 / p.462, checked against the page image). The organising idea: "The fundamental principle of animal motion is that all activity is the result of balance between stability and mobility in the body, with safety relying heavily on how efficiently this dynamic balance is controlled in all sporting movements." Muscles act phasically as movers or tonically as stabilisers, and "Sometimes the roles of the muscles will interchange." The balance "depends on the neuromuscular integration of factors such as strength, endurance and range of movement, as well as the mechanical properties of the tissues involved (in particular, mechanical stiffness and damping ratio)" (PDF 473 / p.462, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "largely", "stability and", "factors", "involved"). Fig 8.7, "The interrelation between stability and mobility in human activity (see Ch 1)," read from the image (PDF 474 / p.463): two boxes, MOBILITY and STABILITY, joined by six bars: Strength, Endurance, Stiffness, Damping Efficiency, Range of Movement, Neuromuscular Control. The text defines stiffness as "the spring constant k in the Hooke's Law equation relating force F to extension x: F = k.x," not "'joint stiffness' which is a popular synonym for inflexibility"; stiffness "also determines the ability of the deformable tissues to store elastic energy (EE = 1/2 k.x²)"; and damping efficiency is "the ability to absorb and dissipate shock or vibration" (PDF 473 / p.462). Strength in the figure "includes all the different types of strength," and endurance means "both muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance."

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: "Neuromuscular processes, including the various reflexes of the body, orchestrate the overall interplay between stability and mobility to produce motor skill," and fatigue in either stabilising or mobilising muscles erodes that control (PDF 473 / p.462). They tie it to PNF: the stability-mobility relationship "forms a vital part of physiotherapeutic PNF ... whose means and methods of physical conditioning may be extended to offer an extensive system of strength training (Fig 8.7)."

**When to apply** — When profiling why an athlete is injury-prone: check the six factors on both the moving and the stabilising side, not strength alone. Inference: novices build mobility before stability in the PNF developmental sequence ([[claim--novices-progress-from-mobility-to-stability-pnf-sequence]]); the figure is the adult, sport version of the same pairing.

**When NOT to apply** — A conceptual diagram with no data or weights for the six factors, so `untested`. The text says "This process is summarised graphically in Figure 3" (PDF 473 / p.462), but the figure printed on the next page is Fig 8.7; "Figure 3" is a misprint or a leftover from an earlier edition. The agonist-antagonist ratio named as a proneness factor is the same kind of ratio the book warns, in 8.7, varies by sport and joint angle ([[claim--weightlifter-extensor-flexor-strength-ratios-far-exceed-the-1-5-norm]]).

**Example** — The authors' own case of role change: stabilisers "will become movers and vice versa" during certain activities, so a muscle trained only as a mover may be unprepared when it must stabilise (PDF 473 / p.462; the second clause is Inference).

**Related** — [[claim--novices-progress-from-mobility-to-stability-pnf-sequence]], [[claim--stiffer-tissue-reaches-its-elastic-limit-sooner-for-the-same-energy-fig-8-8]], [[framework--exercise-stress-by-structural-integrity-four-categories-fig-8-6]], [[claim--weightlifter-extensor-flexor-strength-ratios-far-exceed-the-1-5-norm]]

The organising idea: "The fundamental principle of animal motion is that all activity is the result of balance between stability and mobility in the body, with safety relying heavily on how efficiently this dynamic balance is controlled in all sporting movements." Muscles act phasically as movers or tonically as stabilisers, and "Sometimes the roles of the muscles will interchange." The balance "depends on the neuromuscular integration of factors such as strength, endurance and range of movement, as well as the mechanical properties of the tissues involved (in particular, mechanical stiffness and damping ratio)" (PDF 473 / p.462, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "largely", "stability and", "factors", "involved"). Fig 8.7, "The interrelation between stability and mobility in human activity (see Ch 1)," read from the image (PDF 474 / p.463): two boxes, MOBILITY and STABILITY, joined by six bars: Strength, Endurance, Stiffness, Damping Efficiency, Range of Movement, Neuromuscular Control. Inference: novices build mobility before stability in the PNF developmental sequence ([[claim--novices-progress-from-mobility-to-stability-pnf-sequence]]); the figure is the adult, sport version of the same pairing.

# Absorbing the Same Energy, a Stiffer Tissue Is Driven Closer to Its Elastic Limit (Fig 8.8, Two Springs)

**What it is** — "The role of mechanical stiffness of the soft tissues in overtraining injuries may be appreciated by examining the behaviour of two ideal springs of different stiffness stretching as a result of absorbing the same amount of energy (Fig 8.8)" (PDF 473 / p.462, checked against the page image). "The stiffer spring A, in absorbing the energy E, is forced to its elastic limit at a, whereas the less stiff spring B extends further to C, but reaches nowhere near its elastic limit at b. It is possible, too, that certain individuals may have similar tissue stiffness but higher elastic limits. Again, the result will be a superior ability to absorb energy as imposed for instance on the soft tissues of the knee by running, jumping or squatting (Siff 1982a, b). This analysis is particularly relevant to an understanding of tendon injuries, since much of the muscle activity in running is associated with tensioning of the tendons to store energy, a process which involves little length change in the muscle fibres themselves (Alexander et al, 1967)" (PDF 474 / p.463). Fig 8.8, read from the image at 300 dpi: force on the vertical axis, extension on the horizontal, a horizontal "Elastic Limit" line the same for both springs; line A is steep and meets the limit at point a; line B is shallower and the shaded area under it ends at a vertical line marked c. The caption: "The elastic limit is the same for both springs. The shaded area up to a is the same as the shaded area up to c and represents the energy absorbed, E (Siff 1982a, b)."

**Why it works** — The book states the geometry: equal shaded areas mean equal energy, and the stiffer spring's area reaches the limit first. Inference: for a linear spring the stored energy is E = F²/2k (from F = k.x and EE = 1/2 k.x², PDF 473), so for the same E the peak force F = √(2kE) rises with stiffness k; a stiffer tissue therefore reaches a fixed force limit with less energy absorbed.

**When to apply** — When thinking about why tendons and knee soft tissues fail under repeated running, jumping or squatting: capacity to absorb energy depends on both stiffness and the elastic limit, and the authors suggest some individuals differ in the limit itself. Inference: this supports keeping tendon compliance and elastic storage in mind when stretching or loading tendons ([[heuristic--tendon-stretching-must-preserve-elastic-energy-storage-capacity]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Ideal linear springs, no tissue data, so `untested`; Alexander et al (1967) supports tendon tensioning in running, not the injury claim. The text and figure do not match exactly: the text says B "extends further to C" (capital) and names an elastic limit "at b," but the figure labels the end of B's shaded area with a lowercase c and marks no point b (checked at 300 dpi). Inference: lower stiffness is not simply better; the same section says stiffness also sets elastic-energy storage ([[framework--injury-proneness-and-the-stability-mobility-balance-fig-8-7]]), so the analysis describes a trade-off, and real tissue is viscoelastic, with stiffness that changes with loading rate.

**Example** — The authors' own: soft tissues of the knee absorbing energy in running, jumping or squatting, where a tissue with a higher elastic limit at similar stiffness has "a superior ability to absorb energy" (PDF 474 / p.463).

**Related** — [[heuristic--tendon-stretching-must-preserve-elastic-energy-storage-capacity]], [[framework--injury-proneness-and-the-stability-mobility-balance-fig-8-7]], [[claim--overtraining-injury-parallels-engineering-fatigue-from-overload-and-overuse]]

# The Butterfly Catastrophe Model of Injury (Fig 8.9): Injury Can Arrive Abruptly, Without Warning, Near a Fold

**What it is** — The authors propose renaming the problem: "Instead of referring solely to "overtraining injuries" it might be more valuable to talk of "exercise imbalance injuries". Such a term would embrace any form of unbalanced training, be it excessive, drug assisted or technically faulty" (PDF 474 / p.463, checked against the page image). These injuries "may then be described scientifically on the basis of a qualitative topological model, called Catastrophe Theory by its inventor, Prof Rene Thom (Woodcock & Davis, 1980). Theories which consider overtraining to be a gradual, continuous change from health to injury do not adequately describe the abrupt appearance of some overtraining injuries." The model gives "a behaviour surface, something like a buckled carpet," shaped by control dimensions; the surface describes "the state of health of the joint or body." Four control factors: "Structural Predisposition to Injury: This depends on heredity, structural changes caused by previous exercise, earlier injuries, ageing and so on"; "Technique Stress: This is stress caused by faulty technique, posture and equipment, including footwear"; "Physical Stress: This concerns the exercise load and frequency, current illness, adequacy of sleep, and environmental conditions (such as temperature and altitude)"; and "Psychological Stress" (PDF 474-475 / pp.463-464). One behaviour dimension plus four control dimensions makes "a "butterfly catastrophe"," which needs "a 5 - dimensional drawing, which is impossible"; holding two controls constant "(e.g. psychological stress and technique stress)" gives Fig 8.9, "Butterfly Catastrophe Model of the Injury Process (Siff 1982a, b)" (PDF 475 / p.464). Read from the image: axes Predisposition to Injury (low to high), Physical Stress (low to high) and Physical State (uninjured to injured); regions labelled "normal," "fatigued" and "chronic injury"; points A to H and J.

**Why it works** — The authors walk the paths. An athlete at A moves with rising physical stress toward exhaustion at B, then relaxes "back along path AB towards the initial state A, then to produce re-exertion and repeat the process back and forth within the limits of individual endurance." "A person with a very high predisposition to injury may begin exercising in a state G and without suffering undue stress may reach the threshold H. Any small increase in training load, however, may precipitate him without significant physical warning into the injured state at J. This is vital to remember, since damage may be occurring constantly and insidiously without producing pain signals" (PDF 475 / p.464, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "suffering", "him", "may be"). An athlete starting at C "may progress to the critical point D and become trapped for prolonged periods in a region of the butterfly fold in a state of chronic injury which rest or medical attention may rectify, but only as long as the stressful activity which caused the injury is discontinued" (PDF 475-476 / pp.464-465; the left margin of PDF 476 cuts "a state" and "which", partly reconstructed). A low-predisposition athlete is "not necessarily immune": ignoring exhaustion near B he may "progress towards an injured state such as F," and intense motivation may "even shift the body's initial state from A towards C or increase the extent of the fold by training in a state of residual stress caused by inadequate rest" (PDF 476 / p.465, left margin partly reconstructed: "imbalance", "progress", "even", "residual"). The fold's "extent and location ... depends on the individual and may be influenced, for example, by appropriate supplementary training, medical treatment or ergogenic aids (drugs or supplements)" (PDF 475 / p.464).

**When to apply** — The authors' use: pick any two control dimensions to see how they interact, and "The athlete should rely on objective and subjective tests to identify personal characteristic paths of operation on the behaviour surface and avoid exercising or competing too close to the catastrophe fold (Siff 1982a, b)" (PDF 476 / p.465; "characteristic" and "catastrophe" are cut by the left margin and partly reconstructed). Inference: the model is a way to explain to coaches why a load that was fine last week can injure this week, and why a high-predisposition athlete needs a bigger margin. Eric's review: "No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 143). Inference: this model would not fill that gap, since it gives no quantities to track.

**When NOT to apply** — Qualitative, with no data and no way given to locate an athlete on the surface, so `untested`. The fourth control factor is never defined: the label "Psychological Stress:" is followed directly by the general paragraph on catastrophe structures (PDF 475 / p.464). Point E is marked on Fig 8.9 but not described in the text, so no path through E is given here. The text's first case, "someone with a predisposition to injury" at A, is not placed on the predisposition axis. Inference: the catastrophe framing is a metaphor for nonlinearity; the book does not show that injury data fit a butterfly catastrophe rather than another nonlinear model.

**Example** — The G to H to J path: a highly predisposed athlete trains without undue stress up to the threshold H, and one small load increase drops him "without significant physical warning" into injury at J (PDF 475 / p.464).

**Related** — [[framework--exercise-stress-by-structural-integrity-four-categories-fig-8-6]], [[claim--pain-is-an-unreliable-guide-to-injury-and-exercise-safety]], [[principle--pair-objective-and-subjective-tests-because-rpe-can-miss-a-poor-functional-state]], [[framework--six-fundamental-principles-of-the-injury-process]]

# Nine General Biomechanical Causes of Injury, Expanded Into Eighteen Specific Causes

**What it is** — Under "General Biomechanical Causes of Injury" (PDF 476 / p.465, checked against the page image), nine general causes: "1. The force or stress component (force per unit area of tissue) on some part of the body is excessive in a particular direction (this may be caused by very large mass or very large acceleration); 2. The torque or moment about a certain pivot or joint is excessive; 3. Momentum is too great to be adequately utilised or dissipated; 4. The work load or energy involved over a given period is excessive; 5. The power generated by the muscles is excessive at a particular instant; 6. The strain (change in relative length, ΔL/L) in any tissues is excessive; 7. The mechanical properties of any given tissues are inadequate to handle the loading; 8. The Rate of Force Development (RFD) is excessive at a particular instant; 9. Frictional forces are too large (mat burns or jerkiness) or too small (slipping)." These "may be expanded to identify some more specific causes," 18 bullets: inappropriate warming up or stretching; inappropriate or inefficient patterns of movement; unsafe use of momentum; excessive range of movement for a particular joint; inappropriate phases of muscular tension or relaxation; use of inappropriate soft tissues for a particular action; acceleration or deceleration too great; an excessive load on any part of the body; inappropriate sequences of exercises; excessive exertion during exhaustion, distress, illness or injury; inadequate rest, recovery time or methods of recuperation; inappropriate or faulty equipment; excessive impact forces on body parts making contact with an object or surface; "Inappropriate or inefficient breathing patterns"; excessive duration of any activity; inability to interpret and use proprioceptive and other sensory feedback; inability to "visualize, predict or use feedforward"; and "Inefficient use of breathing or breath-holding patterns" (PDF 476 / p.465; the bullets are paraphrased except where quoted). The left margin of PDF 476 cuts the first letter of a few lines ("The general", "These general"); no list item is affected.

**Why it works** — The general list is mechanics: each item is a physical quantity (stress, torque, momentum, work, power, strain, RFD, friction) or the tissue's capacity to bear it. Inference: the specific list maps programme and coaching choices onto those quantities; for example, poor exercise sequencing or inadequate rest raises the work and fatigue items, and faulty technique shifts stress, torque or strain to the wrong tissue.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when reviewing an injury or a drill: name which physical quantity was excessive, or which tissue was inadequate, before naming the programme cause. Inference: items 5 and 8 (power and RFD "excessive at a particular instant") are a reminder that explosive training carries its own injury mechanism, separate from heavy load.

**When NOT to apply** — Lists with no data or ranking, so `untested`. Two specific bullets nearly repeat each other ("Inappropriate or inefficient breathing patterns" and "Inefficient use of breathing or breath-holding patterns"), so the 18 are really 17 distinct items. Inference: the general list names mechanisms that can be computed only in a lab; in the field it works as a vocabulary, not a measurement.

**Example** — General item 9 in both directions: friction "too large (mat burns or jerkiness) or too small (slipping)" (PDF 476 / p.465).

# Before Cueing a Faulty Movement Pattern, Check the Ten Things That Make Patterns Deviate

**What it is** — "With particular reference to injuries produced by inefficient patterns of movement, one must appreciate that deviations from normal patterns may be caused by:" (PDF 476 / p.465, checked against the page image) "Pain, soreness, stiffness or discomfort"; "Muscle weakness or imbalance between muscle groups"; "Any limitation in the range of joint range of movement in any direction"; "Uncoordinated movement"; "Musculoskeletal changes"; "Fatigue"; "Changes in surface, footwear, equipment or environment"; "Neural changes"; "Visual or balance changes"; "Emotional disturbance" (PDF 476-477 / pp.465-466).

**Why it works** — The authors give the list without a mechanism. Inference: a movement pattern is the output of the body's current state, so a fault seen today may be the athlete compensating for pain, fatigue, a range limit or new shoes rather than a skill error; cueing the fault without removing the cause asks the athlete to override a compensation.

**When to apply** — When a well-learned pattern changes, especially suddenly, ask about these ten before coaching technique. Inference: the first and sixth items (pain and fatigue) are the most common in a team setting and are the ones the next pages tie to injury: pain can reflexly inhibit muscles ([[claim--pain-and-minor-knee-injury-reflexly-inhibit-quadriceps-strength]]).

**When NOT to apply** — A list without data or priorities, so `untested`. "Neural changes" and "Musculoskeletal changes" are broad enough to cover almost anything. A novice's faulty pattern is usually a skill that is not yet learned, which the list does not include.

**Example** — Inference: a sprinter whose stride changes the week the team moves to a new surface; the list's "Changes in surface, footwear, equipment or environment" (PDF 477 / p.466) comes before any cue.

**Related** — [[framework--nine-general-biomechanical-causes-of-injury-and-eighteen-specific-causes]], [[claim--pain-and-minor-knee-injury-reflexly-inhibit-quadriceps-strength]], [[claim--pain-is-an-unreliable-guide-to-injury-and-exercise-safety]]

# Pain Is an Unreliable Guide to Injury and to Whether an Exercise Is Safe

**What it is** — "It is necessary to dispel the belief that all injuries are accompanied by pain. In many cases, such as disintegration of cartilages and hyperflexion damage to the spine, the onset of pain may occur only once the injury has become extensive or serious. Microruptures of soft tissue or similar minor injuries may be unheralded by pain signals until they have accumulated over a sufficiently long period to incapacitate the athlete. Overtraining or regular impact (e.g. caused by running on hard surfaces or by blows to the head in contact sports) are associated with this insidious type of injury process. Individual perception of pain differs markedly among individuals or under different emotional or fatigue states, so that it is unreliable to use the perception of pain to assess the safety of any exercise" (PDF 477 / p.466, checked against the page image; "disintegration", "become", "signals", "regular", "with", "or under" and "safety of" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). The catastrophe model makes the same point: "damage may be occurring constantly and insidiously without producing pain signals. Often pain occurs when it is too late to take evasive action. This is especially true of the cumulative damage caused by years of executing very stressful exercises in terms of either intensity, volume or both" (PDF 475 / p.464).

**Why it works** — Two reasons on the page: some tissue damage accumulates below the pain threshold until it is large, and the threshold itself varies between people and with emotion and fatigue. Inference: a signal that is both late and variable cannot serve as a safety gauge, even though its presence still matters.

**When to apply** — When an athlete or coach treats "it doesn't hurt" as proof that a load or exercise is safe, especially for repeated impact (hard-surface running, head contact) and high-volume or high-intensity work over years. Inference: this is an argument for tracking load and an objective marker over time rather than waiting for symptoms.

**When NOT to apply** — Stated without data or citations, so `untested`. The claim is that absent pain does not prove safety; it is not that pain can be ignored. The next paragraph says the opposite risk matters too: pain reorganises motor control and weakens muscles, so "The importance of dealing with even minor pain, soreness or injury then becomes obvious" (PDF 477 / p.466; see [[claim--pain-and-minor-knee-injury-reflexly-inhibit-quadriceps-strength]]).

**Example** — The authors' examples: cartilage disintegration and spinal hyperflexion damage, where pain "may occur only once the injury has become extensive or serious" (PDF 477 / p.466).

**Related** — [[claim--pain-and-minor-knee-injury-reflexly-inhibit-quadriceps-strength]], [[framework--butterfly-catastrophe-model-of-exercise-imbalance-injury-fig-8-9]], [[heuristic--ten-causes-of-deviation-from-normal-movement-patterns]]

In fact, even if the injury is not accompanied by pain, this can also occur. This is very common with even relatively insubstantial injuries of the knee such as patellar tendinitis, peripatellar pain syndrome or chondromalacia patellae, which significantly reduce the ability of the quadriceps to produce powerful contraction" (PDF 477 / p.466, checked against the page image; "reorganise", "exert", "is not", "of the" and "reduce" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). The importance of dealing with even minor pain, soreness or injury then becomes obvious" (PDF 477 / p.466).

Inference: that this happens "even if the injury is not accompanied by pain" means the trigger is the injury itself, not only the pain, so pain-free does not mean inhibition-free.

**When NOT to apply** — Stokes & Young (1984) and Stauber (1989) are cited, not described, so `untested` on this page. The page gives no rule for how long inhibition lasts or how to reverse it.

**Example** — The book's own: patellar tendinitis, peripatellar pain syndrome or chondromalacia patellae, "relatively insubstantial injuries of the knee," which "significantly reduce the ability of the quadriceps to produce powerful contraction" (PDF 477 / p.466).

type: library-entry
kind: heuristic
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "8.8"
topic: imperfection training
category: [injury-prevention, motor-control, skill, variability]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-10-13
---

# Imperfection Training: Practise Imperfect Execution So the Nervous System Has Contingency Actions Ready

**What it is** — Under "Injury Prevention by Imperfection Training" the authors argue that current prevention "is placed almost exclusively on prevention by means of avoidance of so-called 'dangerous' exercises and excessive volumes or intensities of loading. Unfortunately, this approach is limited in that it tends to neglect the vital aspect of preparation to cope with less than optimal training and competitive situations. All-round sports training must include the capability of coping with unexpected and sub-optimal conditions" (PDF 477 / p.466, checked against the page image; "emphasis is", "excessive", "vital" and "sports" sit on the compressed right margin and are partly reconstructed). In martial arts, parachuting and motor racing, participants are taught to cope with events "that can have serious consequences," and "This type of preparation needs to be adopted far more extensively in all sports so that the athlete is able to anticipate threatening situations, react much more rapidly to unexpected circumstances, take action to avoid or minimise injury, and cope with sub-optimal conditions by practising with imperfectly executed movements" (PDF 477 / p.466). "These strategies are rarely invoked, but they should be a standard item in the training repertoire of every athlete. After all, it is rarely possible to produce perfection of movement every time or to balance one's training loads very precisely, so it is logical to programme the nervous system and brain to respond with effective contingency actions whenever imperfections of movement or accidents occur" (PDF 477-478 / pp.466-467).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: perfect execution and perfectly balanced loading cannot be guaranteed, so the athlete needs trained responses for when they fail. Inference: a recovery response that has been rehearsed under control is faster and better organised than one improvised in a competition fall or a missed lift.

**When to apply** — In skilled lifting and in sports with frequent off-balance or unexpected moments: once the basic pattern is stable, deliberately add controlled imperfection. The authors' example below is from weightlifting. Inference: this should come after basic competency; the authors' own rule for beginners is to "err on the side of conservatism" (PDF 477 / p.466; see [[framework--no-dangerous-exercises-rule-and-its-eight-qualifications]]).

**When NOT to apply** — No data, so `untested`. "Practising with imperfectly executed movements" is not specified as to dose, load or progression. Inference: deliberately unstable positions under heavy load raise risk in their own right, so the book's example (a held snatch, already caught) involves controlling a load in a known position, not missing lifts on purpose. The 8.2 entry covers a related but different point, falling and reaction skills for the risky movements a sport contains ([[principle--prepare-athletes-for-risky-movements-instead-of-avoiding-them]]); this entry is about rehearsing imperfect execution of training movements.

**Example** — "It is not unusual to witness Russian weightlifters holding a snatch overhead in the low squat position and shifting in different directions to move the bar into unstable positions which they are then compelled to control by astute postural adjustments" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**Related** — [[principle--prepare-athletes-for-risky-movements-instead-of-avoiding-them]] (8.2), [[framework--no-dangerous-exercises-rule-and-its-eight-qualifications]]

"heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic": "[[claim--overtraining-injury-parallels-engineering-fatigue-from-overload-and-overuse]] (8.8: recalls the acute overreaching and chronic overtraining distinction)",
"claim--vorobyev-mean-training-weight-by-bodymass-and-qualification": "[[case-study--vorobyev-vertical-jump-rises-with-weightlifter-qualification-table-8-13]] (8.7: Vorobyev's vertical jump by class)",
"principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy": "[[case-study--vorobyev-jerk-dip-parameters-by-bar-weight-table-8-12]] (8.7: pause in the jerk dip kept under 0.25 s)",
}
special = {
"principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting": " From 8.7: [[case-study--shtanga-functional-pressure-test-ulchenko-weightlifters]] (a forced breath-hold pressure test, to which this entry's cardiac caution applies).",

    if "[[" + txt.split("[[")[-1].split("]]")[0] + "]]" in s: print("skip", stem); continue
    p.write_text(s.rstrip("\n") + "\n\n" + txt + "\n"); print("also", stem)
def rel_para_end(lines):
    i = next(k for k,l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("**Related** —"))
    j = i
    while j+1 < len(lines) and lines[j+1].strip() != "" and not lines[j+1].startswith("**"):
        j += 1
    return j
for stem, txt in list(rel.items()) + list(special.items()):
    p = D / f"{stem}.md"; s = p.read_text()
    link = txt[txt.index("[["):txt.index("]]")+2]
    if link in s: print("skip", stem); continue
    lines = s.split("\n"); j = rel_para_end(lines); l = lines[j].rstrip()
    if stem in special:
        lines[j] = l + txt
    elif l.endswith("."):
        lines[j] = l[:-1] + ", " + txt + "."
    else:
        lines[j] = l + ", " + txt
    p.write_text("\n".join(lines)); print("rel", stem, "line", j+1)

# McDougall's Four Values of Testing and Seven Characteristics of an Effective Testing Programme

**What it is** — Section 8.7 opens by restating that "the most specific test of all is performance in the actual sporting event. All other tests have varying degrees of correlation with performance or selected actions in the given sport" (PDF 468 / p.457, checked against the page image). The author, writing in the first person ("my Canadian colleague, Dr Duncan Mc Dougall"), then summarises McDougall et al (1982). Four values of "suitable, well-planned tests": (1) "They identify individual strengths and weaknesses and provide data for determining the baseline for training programmes"; (2) "They provide feedback on the effectiveness of training programmes"; (3) "They provide information on the athlete's state of health"; (4) "They provide an educational process which teaches the athlete to understand more competently his/her body and the demands of the sport." Seven characteristics of an effective programme: (1) "The variables which are tested must be directly relevant to the given sport"; (2) "The tests must be valid (test what it claims to), reliable and reproducible"; (3) "The testing procedures must be as sport specific as possible"; (4) "The testing situation must be rigidly controlled"; (5) "Testing must be repeated at regular, appropriate intervals"; (6) "The tests must respect the athlete's human rights (including ethics, confidentiality and risks)"; (7) "The results must be interpreted in understandable language directly to the athlete and coach" (PDF 468 / p.457). The author then says the section will not "reiterate what has already been written" by testing authorities and will "simply ... provide information which is not readily available" (PDF 468 / p.457). The book prints the name both as "Mc Dougall" and "McDougall"; the OCR's "Me Dougall" is an artifact.

**Why it works** — The book gives no separate mechanism; the lists rest on the opening point that every test other than competition is only a correlate of performance. Inference: items 1 and 3 keep that correlate as close to the sport as possible; items 2, 4 and 5 make a change between two test dates attributable to training rather than to noise or a changed protocol; item 7 makes the result usable by the people who change the programme.

**When to apply** — When building or auditing a test battery, or deciding whether to keep a test. Eric's review: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Eric's review: "Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 57, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's review: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 34, Explicit). Inference: McDougall's items 1, 4 and 5 match these lines; the baseline lines quoted here say nothing about item 6 (ethics and confidentiality) or item 7 (explaining results directly to the athlete).

**When NOT to apply** — The lists are a checklist, not evidence that testing improves results; McDougall et al (1982) is cited, not described, and `supported` rests on it being a named, standard text the author endorses. Inference: items 1 and 3 ("as sport specific as possible") pull against item 2 (reliability), since the most sport-like tests are often the hardest to control; Eric's own battery leans on general, reliable tests ("bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max", `docs/method-baseline.md`, line 58). The four values say what tests can "provide", not that every test must serve all four.

**Example** — The author applies item 3 at once to the vertical jump: because results "correlate best with conditions which are most similar to that of the test", it is "useful to repeat the test with the non-dominant hand or in the frontal plane with the athlete using both hands" (PDF 468 / p.457). See [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]].

**Related** — [[claim--laboratory-tests-cannot-predict-performance-or-select-talent]], [[heuristic--test-monthly-under-constant-conditions-and-compare-with-targets]] (constant conditions, monthly comparison, 6.16), [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]]

# Vertical Jump Rises With Weightlifting Qualification: 57.3 cm in Novices to 85.5 cm in Elite (Table 8.13)

**What it is** — Table 8.13, "Mean dynamic start Vertical Jump for Olympic Weightlifters from all divisions (Vorobyev, 1978)" (PDF 469 / p.458, every cell read from the page image): Novice 57.3 cm; Class III 58.1; Class II 65.3; Class I 67.8; Master of Sport 72.3; Elite 85.5. The book offers these as "Guidelines concerning the vertical jump height for different levels of competitive weightlifter." It adds two individual results it calls "noteworthy": a former high-jump world-record holder with a best vertical jump of 102 cm, and a superheavyweight champion weightlifter who reached 91 cm "despite his enormous bodymass (over 140kg)." Its reading: "these competitors displayed exceptional absolute vertical jumps, as well as excellent relative vertical jumps (height per unit bodymass) and leg power" (PDF 469 / p.458, partly reconstructed at the right margin: "high jump", "champion", "vertical"). The two athletes are named in the book; the names are not carried here.

**Why it works** — The book gives no mechanism. Inference: the weightlifting classes are ranked by lifted totals that depend on explosive leg extension, so a rising jump with class is what one would expect if the jump and the lifts share that quality; the table is cross-sectional, so it shows association, not that training raised the jump.

**When to apply** — As a rough reference when testing weightlifters with a dynamic-start jump (the book's condition 4 or 5 in [[heuristic--vertical-jump-test-five-start-conditions-and-knee-angle-profile]]). Inference: the biggest step is from Master of Sport to Elite (13.2 cm), while Novice to Class III differs by only 0.8 cm, so the jump separates the top of the sport far better than the bottom.

**When NOT to apply** — Means only, with no spread, sample size or test details beyond "dynamic start"; whether arms were used is not stated. Weightlifters "from all divisions" are pooled, so heavy and light lifters sit in one mean, and the book's own point is that relative jump (per bodymass) matters. Inference: these 1978 Soviet norms are not norms for team-sport athletes or for force-plate jump height, which is computed differently from a reach test.

**Example** — Elite weightlifters averaged 85.5 cm against 72.3 cm for Masters of Sport (PDF 469 / p.458).

**Related** — [[claim--vorobyev-mean-training-weight-by-bodymass-and-qualification]] (Vorobyev's by-class training data), [[case-study--vorobyev-jerk-dip-parameters-by-bar-weight-table-8-12]], [[claim--laboratory-tests-cannot-predict-performance-or-select-talent]]

# Nine General Biomechanical Causes of Injury, Expanded Into Eighteen Specific Causes

**What it is** — Under "General Biomechanical Causes of Injury" (PDF 476 / p.465, checked against the page image), nine general causes: "1. The force or stress component (force per unit area of tissue) on some part of the body is excessive in a particular direction (this may be caused by very large mass or very large acceleration); 2. The torque or moment about a certain pivot or joint is excessive; 3. Momentum is too great to be adequately utilised or dissipated; 4. The work load or energy involved over a given period is excessive; 5. The power generated by the muscles is excessive at a particular instant; 6. The strain (change in relative length, ΔL/L) in any tissues is excessive; 7. The mechanical properties of any given tissues are inadequate to handle the loading; 8. The Rate of Force Development (RFD) is excessive at a particular instant; 9. Frictional forces are too large (mat burns or jerkiness) or too small (slipping)." These "may be expanded to identify some more specific causes," 18 bullets: inappropriate warming up or stretching; inappropriate or inefficient patterns of movement; unsafe use of momentum; excessive range of movement for a particular joint; inappropriate phases of muscular tension or relaxation; use of inappropriate soft tissues for a particular action; acceleration or deceleration too great; an excessive load on any part of the body; inappropriate sequences of exercises; excessive exertion during exhaustion, distress, illness or injury; inadequate rest, recovery time or methods of recuperation; inappropriate or faulty equipment; excessive impact forces on body parts making contact with an object or surface; "Inappropriate or inefficient breathing patterns"; excessive duration of any activity; inability to interpret and use proprioceptive and other sensory feedback; inability to "visualize, predict or use feedforward"; and "Inefficient use of breathing or breath-holding patterns" (PDF 476 / p.465; the bullets are paraphrased except where quoted). The left margin of PDF 476 cuts the first letter of a few lines ("The general", "These general"); no list item is affected.

**Why it works** — The general list is mechanics: each item is a physical quantity (stress, torque, momentum, work, power, strain, RFD, friction) or the tissue's capacity to bear it. Inference: the specific list maps programme and coaching choices onto those quantities; for example, poor exercise sequencing or inadequate rest raises the work and fatigue items, and faulty technique shifts stress, torque or strain to the wrong tissue.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when reviewing an injury or a drill: name which physical quantity was excessive, or which tissue was inadequate, before naming the programme cause. Inference: items 5 and 8 (power and RFD "excessive at a particular instant") are a reminder that explosive training carries its own injury mechanism, separate from heavy load.

**When NOT to apply** — Lists with no data or ranking, so `untested`. Two specific bullets nearly repeat each other ("Inappropriate or inefficient breathing patterns" and "Inefficient use of breathing or breath-holding patterns"), so the 18 are really 17 distinct items. Inference: the general list names mechanisms that can be computed only in a lab; in the field it works as a vocabulary, not a measurement.

**Example** — General item 9 in both directions: friction "too large (mat burns or jerkiness) or too small (slipping)" (PDF 476 / p.465).
